https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.paragraph: Minutes of the Troy Board of Education regular meeting of October 20, 2020, held at the Services Building, 4420 Livernois, and livestreamed via Zoom Webinar, presented for approval as item 5.B on the November 17, 2020 agenda. The Board honored fifty-two 2021 National Merit Scholarship Semifinalists, accepted the district's audited 2020 financial statements from Plante Moran, and approved purchases from Presidio Networked Solutions Group and IMBranded. The most contentious action was a disclaiming motion stating that the actions of Trustee Hammond are not the actions of the Troy Board of Education, adopted on a 4-3 roll call.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.page:
Meeting and attendance
- Regular meeting of the Troy Board of Education, October 20, 2020, Services Building, 4420 Livernois, Troy, Michigan, livestreamed via Zoom Webinar with public notice posted so community members could participate remotely.
- President Schmidt called the meeting to order at 7:10 p.m.; the start was delayed by technical/audio difficulties. The meeting adjourned at 11:38 p.m.
- Board members physically present with Mr. Schmidt: Anne, Gottlieb, Hammond, Hauff, Philippart, and Wilson. Also present: Superintendent Machesky and administrators Birmingham, DiPilato, Pagel, and West.
- Approximately 75 additional members of the audience attended via Zoom Webinar, along with four student representatives to the Board and Donna Hanson and Michael Walsh of Plante Moran.
- Minutes respectfully submitted by Gary N. Hauff, Secretary, Troy Board of Education (GH/jh).

Recognition
- TSD Mission Moment: Kris Griffor, Assistant Superintendent, Elementary Instruction, introduced the TSD CARE Company, recognizing Tim Fulcher, Dawn Wyatt, and CARE Co. staff for providing childcare to TSD staff while many centers were closed during the pandemic. Dawn Wyatt recognized Sui Chu, Gina Kitchen, Ally Larkins, and Linda Smith, and thanked Dr. Erin Detmer for providing space at Leonard Elementary School.
- 2021 National Merit Scholarship Semifinalists: Christine DiPilato, Assistant Superintendent, Secondary Instruction, reported that more than one million students nationwide from some 21,000 high schools entered the program and only 16,000 seniors are selected as semifinalists. A resolution honored fifty-two Troy semifinalists, who reached that status by scoring in the top one and one-half percent on the PSAT. Copies were to be presented at a virtual reception on November 4th; the resolution was signed the twentieth day of October 2020 and adopted 7-0.
- Michigan Association of School Boards awards: Board Secretary Gary Hauff received the President's Award, the highest level of achievement, requiring 29 advanced classes and a minimum of 1,383 education credits; Don Wotruba, Executive Director of MASB in Lansing, presented it in Troy. Trustee Dr. Nancy Philippart was recognized for 12 years of service.

Numbered actions
| Res. | Item | Vote |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 20-076 | Consent agenda items A through I | 7-0 |
| 20-077 | Personnel recommendations (new hires) | 7-0 |
| 20-078 | TESA/MEA/NEA tentative agreement ratification | 7-0 |
| 20-079 | Audited 2020 financial statements accepted | 7-0 |
| 20-080 | Adult Education technology purchase, $54,456.00 | 7-0 |
| 20-081 | PPE purchase, $44,851.80 | 7-0 |
| 20-082 | Reconfirmation of COVID-19 Preparedness & Response Plan | 6-1 |
| 20-083 | Disclaiming motion regarding Trustee Hammond | 4-3 |

Other business
- Mrs. Hammond asked that the Reconfirmation of the COVID-19 Preparedness & Response Plan be removed from the consent agenda; Mr. Schmidt moved it to Other.
- Public communication: Katie Gorman, Joe Pettinato, Amber Barbieri, and Alec Peeples, all residents of Troy, addressed the Board on the Hamilton principal and staff, Board ethics, transparency, and support for teachers.
- Plante Moran presented the 2019-2020 fiscal year audit, first shown in draft at the October 16th Board Workshop, reporting no findings or questioned costs.
- Superintendent's update featured elementary and secondary principals describing in-seat and remote learning.
- Student representatives Nathania Nartey (Athens High), Pranay Gupta (International Academy-East), and Sejal Patil (Troy High) reported; Carlton Thomas (Troy College & Career High School) was not present.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
Minutes of the regular meeting of the Troy Board of Education held October 20, 2020 in the Services Building at 4420 Livernois and livestreamed via Zoom Webinar, with a public notice posted to allow community members to participate remotely. The minutes were placed on the November 17, 2020 Board agenda as item 5.B for approval.

Call to order and attendance. President Schmidt called the meeting to order at 7:10 p.m.; the start was delayed due to technical/audio difficulties. In addition to Mr. Schmidt, Board members physically present were Anne, Gottlieb, Hammond, Hauff, Philippart, and Wilson. Also present were Superintendent Machesky and administrators Birmingham, DiPilato, Pagel, and West. Approximately 75 additional members of the audience were present via Zoom Webinar, as well as four student representatives to the Board and Donna Hanson and Michael Walsh from Plante Moran.

Recognition - TSD Mission Moment: CARE Company Staff. Kris Griffor, Assistant Superintendent, Elementary Instruction, introduced the TSD CARE Company as the month's Mission Moment. She recognized Tim Fulcher, Dawn Wyatt, and the CARE Co. staff and thanked them for providing quality childcare service to TSD staff members, noting that many childcare centers were closed due to the pandemic. Dawn Wyatt introduced her team and recognized Sui Chu, Gina Kitchen, Ally Larkins, and Linda Smith, and thanked Dr. Erin Detmer for providing the space in Leonard Elementary School to hold the program.

Recognition - 2021 National Merit Scholarship Semifinalists. Mrs. Christine DiPilato, Assistant Superintendent, Secondary Instruction, announced that more than one million students nationwide from some 21,000 high schools entered the National Merit Scholarship Program, and that only 16,000 of these seniors are selected as semifinalists. The resolution recited that National Merit students reach semifinalist status by scoring in the top one and one-half percent on the National Preliminary Scholastic Aptitude Test (PSAT) and earning comparable scores on the Scholastic Aptitude Test (SAT). Moved by Dr. Wilson and supported by Dr. Philippart, the Board adopted a resolution commending fifty-two Troy School District semifinalists: Nina Aitas, Harika Billa, Marcus Chung, Poulomi Dey, Sneha Dinda, Prashanti Donthireddy, Alaina Favret, Archita Girmannagari, Annie He, Madhavan Iyengar, Diksha Iyer, Shruti Jain, Mahith Kanuri, Achyuth Kashyap, Arjun Kashyap, Raj Khuperkar, Heeweon Kim, Minseong Kim, Armol Kirtane, Krishna Kottai, Nathan Kovacs, Sophia Liang, Elliot Liu, Shifa Malik, Sandhya Manivasagam, Esha Munagala, Parvathi Nagappala, Kishan Patel, Aarti Phatke, Prajna Polamarasetti, Lauryn Prokup, Sohil Ramachandra, Navneet Ramadurai, Swarith Reddy, Surya Sanjay, Nicholas Simon, Sabrina Song, Matthew Villavicencio, Sohan Vittalam, Allison Wei, Josiah Wong, Jasmine Wu, Alexander Xu, Sarah Xu, Lily Yang, Ruicheng Yang, Dorothy Yin, Michael Young, Darren Zeng, Anna Zhao, Katherine Zhao, and Erik Zhou. Copies of the resolution were to be presented to the students at a virtual reception on November 4th. The resolution was signed this twentieth day of October 2020 and carried on a roll call with Philippart, Schmidt, Wilson, Anne, Gottlieb, Hammond, and Hauff all voting Yes.

Recognition - Michigan Association of School Boards awards. The Board honored Secretary Gary Hauff for receiving the President's Award, described as the highest level of achievement, which requires a Board member to complete 29 advanced classes and a minimum of 1,383 education credits. Don Wotruba, Executive Director of the Michigan Association of School Boards in Lansing, came to Troy to honor Mr. Hauff with the award Friday morning. Trustee Dr. Nancy Philippart was recognized for 12 years of dedicated service on the Board.

Additions and deletions. Mrs. Hammond requested that the Reconfirmation of the COVID-19 Preparedness & Response Plan be removed from the consent agenda and placed as a regular agenda item for discussion; Mr. Schmidt agreed to move that item to Other.

Public communication. Katie Gorman, resident of Troy, spoke about the Hamilton principal and the job the staff is doing keeping students safe, and said discussion at the last Board meeting should have been conducted in closed session rather than a public meeting. Joe Pettinato, resident of Troy, expressed appreciation for the Board's response during the past few months and mentioned Elizabeth Hammond's leadership and engagement. Amber Barbieri, resident of Troy, addressed Board ethics and thanked Mrs. Hammond for advocating on residents' behalf. Alec Peeples, resident of Troy, addressed transparency and ethics and asked for support of open public discourse.

General - consent agenda, resolution 20-076. Moved by Mr. Hauff and supported by Mr. Gottlieb, the Board approved items A through I: A. Minutes of the September 1, 2020 Board of Education Workshop; B. Minutes of the September 1, 2020 Special Board of Education Meeting; C. Minutes of the September 15, 2020 Board of Education Meeting; D. Minutes of the September 15, 2020 Closed Session Meeting; E. Minutes of the September 29, 2020 Special Board of Education Meeting; F. Treasurer's Report - August 2020; G. Oakland County CARES Act Distribution Interlocal Agreement; H. Safe-Ed Contract Extension; and I. Clean-Ed Contract Extension. Roll call: Schmidt, Wilson, Anne, Gottlieb, Hammond, Hauff, and Philippart Yes. Yes: 7, No: 0.

Personnel, resolution 20-077. The Board approved the personnel recommendations as stated, with new hires Breanna Thacker, Nicole Wilson, Hannah Tout, Jodie Seilheimer, and Emily Surzyn. Roll call: Wilson, Anne, Gottlieb, Hammond, Hauff, Philippart, and Schmidt Yes. Yes: 7, No: 0.

TESA contract extension, resolution 20-078. Moved by Mrs. Anne and supported by Mrs. Hammond, the Board ratified and adopted the tentative agreement reached on September 30, 2020 between representatives of the Troy Board of Education and the Troy Educational Secretaries Association/MEA/NEA for the period of July 1, 2020 through June 30, 2024. Roll call: Anne, Gottlieb, Hammond, Hauff, Philippart, Schmidt, and Wilson Yes. Yes: 7, No: 0.

Business - 2019/2020 Audit Report, resolution 20-079. Ms. Donna Hanson and Mr. Michael Walsh from Plante Moran presented on the audit of the 2019-2020 fiscal year; a draft copy of the District's Audit Report had been presented in detail to the Board at the October 16th Board Workshop. They reported there were no findings or questioned costs. Governmental funds revenue and expenditures were reviewed, as well as student population and foundation allowance. The economic impact of the pandemic and MPSERS challenges, and changes in federal funding such as the Coronavirus Relief Funds, Elementary and Secondary School Emergency Relief Funds, and Child Care Relief Funds, were discussed at length. Moved by Dr. Philippart and supported by Mr. Gottlieb, the Board accepted and approved the Troy School District's audited 2020 financial statements as presented by Plante Moran. Roll call: Anne, Gottlieb, Hammond, Hauff, Philippart, Schmidt, and Wilson Yes. Yes: 7, No: 0.

Adult Education Technology Purchase, resolution 20-080. The Board approved the purchase of laptops and carts from Presidio Networked Solutions Group in the amount of $54,456.00, approved as an expenditure of the General Fund. Roll call: Gottlieb, Hammond, Hauff, Philippart, Schmidt, Wilson, and Anne Yes. Yes: 7, No: 0.

PPE Purchase, resolution 20-081. The Board approved the purchase of acrylic shields and graphics from IMBranded in the amount of $44,851.80, approved as an expenditure of the General Fund. Roll call: Hammond, Hauff, Philippart, Schmidt, Wilson, Anne, and Gottlieb Yes. Yes: 7, No: 0.

Superintendent's update. Dr. Machesky asked Kris Griffor, Assistant Superintendent, Elementary Instruction, and Christine DiPilato, Assistant Superintendent, Secondary Instruction, to share an update on learning at both the elementary and secondary level. Ms. Griffor introduced Bemis Principal Jeremey Whan, Hill Principal Shari Pawlus, Leonard Principal Dr. Erin Detmer, and Morse Principal Stephanie Zendler, who gave examples of learning happening in their buildings. Ms. DiPilato introduced Smith Principal Chris Mueller and Boulan Park Principal Tony Morse to describe how middle school students had transitioned back to in-seat learning. Further discussion followed among Board and administration about students returning to in-seat and remote learning.

Reconfirmation of the COVID-19 Preparedness & Response Plan, resolution 20-082. Governor Whitmer's Executive Order 2020-142 provides a structure to support Michigan schools planning for the return of Pre-K through Post High School education in the fall; under the order districts must adopt a COVID-19 Preparedness and Response Plan addressing the phases of the Michigan Safe Start Plan, submit a reconfirmation plan to the Board monthly, and post the Preparedness Plan on the district website home page for public access. Moved by Dr. Philippart and supported by Dr. Wilson, the Board approved the District's Reconfirmation. Roll call: Hauff, Philippart, Schmidt, Wilson, Anne, and Gottlieb Yes; Hammond No. Yes: 6, No: 1.

Reports from student representatives. Nathania Nartey, Student Representative for Athens High School; Pranay Gupta, Student Representative for the International Academy-East; and Sejal Patil, Student Representative for Troy High School, each shared updates. Carlton Thomas, Student Representative for Troy College & Career High School, was not present.

Board member ethics violation, resolution 20-083. Dr. Wilson and Dr. Philippart shared a PowerPoint presentation explaining the role of a Board member, covering Board governance, the National School Boards Association Code of Ethics, the Code of Ethics outlined in the TSD Policy Manual, censure, and disclaiming acts of individual Board members. They presented examples of an ethics violation and provided excerpts of social media posts and a letter from the Troy Education Association, stating that given social media posts made by Trustee Hammond, who is seen as a representative of the Board, the community's interpretation of recent actions may be misconstrued as representing the Board and District. Moved by Dr. Philippart and supported by Dr. Wilson, the motion declared that the actions of Trustee Hammond are not the actions of the Troy Board of Education and that the community be alerted that unless specifically authorized by motion of the Board, Trustee Hammond's opinions and actions are as an individual community member and should not be construed as representing the Troy Board of Education. Mr. Schmidt gave each Board member the opportunity to speak before voting. Roll call: Philippart, Schmidt, Wilson, and Hauff Yes; Anne, Gottlieb, and Hammond No. Yes: 4, No: 3.

Adjournment. The meeting adjourned at 11:38 p.m. Respectfully submitted by Gary N. Hauff, Secretary, Troy Board of Education (GH/jh).

Solicitation
- Bid No. 9909, Exterior Signage at Athens High School, Learning Center and Early Childcare Center, Troy School District. Purchasing Department, 1140 Rankin, Troy, MI 48083.
- Specifications available through the district website under Business Services / Purchasing and posted on BuildingConnected at https://app.buildingconnected.com/public/5f0dc09564fd95003450f194 by November 4, 2020 at 5:00 PM local time.
- Sealed bids submitted only through BuildingConnected; no physical, oral, email, telephonic, or telegraphic proposals. Due no later than 11:00 AM Wednesday, November 4, 2020; public opening immediately after via meet.google.com/dns-ibvf-oif.
- No pre-bid walk through. The invitation sets a question deadline of noon, Wednesday, October 28, 2020 (fax 248.823.4077, email PurchasingOffice@troy.k12.mi.us), while Instruction 4 states questions must be received no later than noon, Wednesday, November 28, 2020. Instruction 1 also carries over language referring to Bid No. 9906 Niles Center Demolition.
- Award recommendation to the Board of Education at the regular meeting of Tuesday, November 17, 2020.

Work scope
| Site | Address | Work |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Troy Learning Center | 1522 Big Beaver Road, Troy, MI 48083 | New exterior signage |
| Troy Early Childhood Care | 201 West Square Lake Road, Troy, MI 48098 | New exterior signage |
| Athens High School | 4333 John R Road, Troy, MI 48085 | Remove and replace exterior signage; masonry structure maintained and modified as required |

The contractor is responsible for excavation and concrete, City and State permits, final electrical connection, COVID-19 procedures per the Troy School District website and Oakland County, removal of soil spoils, site restoration, and waste removal. The base bid must include a $5,000 allowance at the Owner's discretion. Electrical is excluded. The proposal form breaks out Athens High School, Learning Center, Early Childcare Center, Base Bid, and Bond amounts and requires five recent references.

Bidding requirements
- Bid bond or certified check for not less than five percent of the bid; unsuccessful bidders' security returned within ten days.
- Performance and payment bonds of 100% of the bid for proposals of $50,000 or more per MCL 129.201; bond company must be a Michigan licensed carrier with an excellent or superior AM Best rating.
- Notarized familial disclosure per MCL 380.1267 and Iran Economic Sanctions Act certification under Public Act 517 of 2012; false certification carries a civil penalty of not more than $250,000.00 or two times the contract amount, whichever is greater, plus three years of bid ineligibility.
- Bidders must have at least five years of experience; bids may not be withdrawn until 45 days after bid opening; contract executed within fourteen days of notice of selection.
- Insurance: Employer's Liability, Comprehensive General Liability, Owner's Contractor's Protective, and Automobile Liability each at $1,000,000, with 60 days written notice of change or cancellation.
- Criminal history and background checks required under MCL 380.1230 et seq. for personnel on district premises more than one continuous week.

Technical specification
- Internally illuminated two-sided aluminum pylon signs, basis of design ASI Sign Systems, Inc. of Irving, Texas; 120 V, 60 Hz, 1 phase, 15 A; box depth 1'-6"; five-year special warranty from Substantial Completion; wind load 120 MPH (3 sec gust).
- LED message centers, basis of design Thinksign Model Xtreme V-2 16 mm display, or Daktronics, Spectrum, or approved equal; full color, 4.4" character height, minimum 60 pixel rows by 150 pixel columns, IP-67 sealed modules, 4G or 5G lifetime cellular communications.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
Complete bid package issued by the Troy School District Purchasing Department for Bid No. 9909, Exterior Signage at Athens High School, Learning Center and Early Childcare Center. The package contains the Invitation to Bid, Instructions to Bidders, scope of work, proposal form, familial disclosure and Iran Economic Sanctions certifications, acceptance of proposal form, and the Division-level Exterior Signage technical specification, followed by aerial location imagery.

Invitation to Bid. The Troy School District will receive firm, sealed bids for all labor, material, equipment and all other services to complete Bid No. 9909. Specifications and proposal forms are obtainable online at http://www.troy.k12.mi.us under the Business Services tab, then Purchasing. Bid documents were to be placed on BuildingConnected at https://app.buildingconnected.com/public/5f0dc09564fd95003450f194 by November 4, 2020 at 5:00 PM local time. Sealed bids must be submitted through that BuildingConnected link; no physical bids are accepted, and no oral, email, telephonic or telegraphic proposals are considered. Bids were due no later than 11:00 AM Wednesday, November 4, 2020, and publicly opened immediately following the close of receiving bids at the virtual meeting link meet.google.com/dns-ibvf-oif. No pre-bid walk through was scheduled. Questions were to be submitted in writing only and answered by addendum to all interested parties, with the invitation setting a deadline of noon, Wednesday October 28, 2020, questions faxed to 248.823.4077 or emailed as a Word document to PurchasingOffice@troy.k12.mi.us. The Instructions to Bidders section carries a conflicting statement that questions must be received no later than noon, Wednesday, November 28, 2020, and its opening paragraph retains boilerplate referring to Bid No. 9906 Niles Center Demolition. The issuing office is the Purchasing Department, Troy School District, 1140 Rankin, Troy, MI 48083. The recommendation for award was to be submitted to the Board of Education at the regular Board of Education meeting to be held on Tuesday, November 17, 2020.

Statutory and bonding requirements. All bidders must provide familial disclosure in compliance with MCL 380.1267, attached to the bid proposal as a sworn and notarized statement disclosing any familial relationship between the owner or any employee of the bidder and any member of the Troy School Board or the Troy School District's Superintendent. A sworn and notarized affidavit of compliance for the Iran Economic Sanctions Act, certifying compliance with Public Act 517 of 2012, must accompany all proposals; a false certification carries a civil penalty of not more than $250,000.00 or two times the amount of the contract or proposed contract, whichever is greater, plus the cost of the District's investigation and reasonable attorney fees, and renders the person ineligible to bid for three years. In accordance with Michigan Compiled Laws Section 129.201, successful bidders whose proposals are $50,000 or more for any bid category must furnish a U.S. Treasury Listed Company Performance and Payment Bond in the amount of 100% of their bid, with the cost of the bond identified within each proposal. A bid bond or certified check for not less than five percent of the bid amount must accompany each bid; the security of each unsuccessful bidder is returned within ten days after award. A performance bond is required if the project cost exceeds $50,000 and must be listed separately on the proposal form as an individual line item. Within fourteen days after written notice of selection, treated as notice to proceed, the successful bidder must enter into a contract and file bonds equal to 100% of the full contract sum, from a bond company listed by the State of Michigan as a licensed carrier with an excellent or superior rating from AM Best Company. The Troy Board of Education reserves the right to accept or reject any or all bids in whole or in part, to award to other than the low bidder, and to waive irregularities.

Bidder qualifications and commercial terms. Bidders must be reputable, recognized organizations with at least five years of successful experience on work of this type and scope. Material and equipment are guaranteed free from defects in workmanship and materials for no less than two years from date of receipt or installation, with manufacturer warranty prevailing where longer, and defective items replaced or repaired within seven working days at vendor expense. No proposal may be withdrawn until after 45 days after bid opening; the acceptance of proposal form states the undersigned will execute a contract if notified of acceptance within thirty days after opening. The successful bidder holds bid prices firm for all purchase orders for approximately one full year. The contractor obtains and pays for all permits, assessments, fees and other charges, and provides the District all permit paperwork at completion. Troy School District is not automatically exempt from State of Michigan Sales and Use Taxes; taxes on materials permanently attached or incorporated into realty are paid by the vendor.

Insurance and safety. The contractor must maintain Worker's Compensation Insurance with statutory limits and Employer's Liability Insurance with a minimum limit of $1,000,000 each occurrence; Comprehensive General Liability with a minimum combined single limit of $1,000,000 per occurrence and $1,000,000 aggregate, endorsed for sixty days written notice of material change, cancellation or non-renewal; an Owner's Contractor's Protective Policy in the name of the Owner at a minimum combined single limit of $1,000,000 per occurrence; and Automobile Liability covering owned, hired and non-owned vehicles at a minimum combined single limit of $1,000,000 each occurrence under the Michigan no-fault Insurance Law. Policies must be issued by domestic on-shore companies licensed in Michigan with an A rating by AM Best. Compliance is required with the School Safety Initiative Legislation, MCL 380.1230, 80.1230a, 380.1230c, 380.1230d and 380.1230g; all installation personnel including subcontractors working on District premises more than one continuous week must undergo criminal history and background checks within a year of the beginning of the project, at the bidder's expense, with written documentation verifying that no personnel have a listed offense. The listed offenses enumerated include MCL 750.145a, 750.145b, 750.145c, 750.158, 750.167(1)(f), 750.335a, 750.338, 750.338a, 750.338b, 750.349, 750.350, 750.448, 750.455, 750.520b, 750.520c, 750.520d, 750.520e, 750.520g, and 750.10a. Additional provisions cover termination by the District for convenience, Equal Opportunity Employer status under Executive Order 11246, the Michigan Right to Know Law, the EPA Asbestos Hazard Emergency Response Act contractor notification forms, and presumed lead-containing materials requiring compliance with 29 CFR Part 1926.62 of the OSHA Lead Construction Standard, Part 603 of the Michigan State Standards, at contractor expense.

Work scope. The bid covers exterior signage at Athens High School, Learning Center and Early Childcare Center, on a line item lump sum basis: new exterior signage at Troy Learning Center, 1522 Big Beaver Road, Troy, MI 48083; new exterior signage at Troy Early Childhood Care, 201 West Square Lake Road, Troy, MI 48098; and removal and replacement of exterior signage at Athens High School, 4333 John R Road, Troy, MI 48085, where the masonry structure will be maintained and modified as required for proper installation. The contractor is responsible for all necessary excavation and concrete, all permits from City and State, final electrical connection to the sign, coordination with the Owner so as not to affect the buildings or operations, compliance with COVID-19 procedures noted on the Troy School District website and Oakland County, removal of soil spoils, concrete clean up and site restoration, and removal of all waste from the site. The base bid must include an allowance of $5,000 to be used at the Owner's discretion. Electrical is an excluded item. The proposal form requires separate amounts for Athens High School, Learning Center, Early Childcare Center, Base Bid and Bond, plus five recent references, preferably school districts.

Exterior signage specification. The section covers internally illuminated pylon signs and LED message centers, with delegated design by a qualified professional engineer for sign structure and anchorage. Structural performance requires a wind load of 120 MPH (3 sec gust) and thermal movement allowance for a temperature change of 120 deg F ambient and 180 deg F material surfaces; accessibility complies with ICC A117.1 and electrical components are listed and labeled as defined in NFPA 70. Verification samples include pylon sign samples not less than 12 inches square and 8-inch variable component material samples. The special warranty period is five years from date of Substantial Completion, covering deterioration of finishes beyond normal weathering, deterioration of embedded graphic image, delamination of sheet materials, and failure of the LED message center display.

Pylon signs use a basis of design of ASI Sign Systems, Inc., ASI Signage Innovations, 8181 Jetstar Drive, Suite 100, Irving, Texas 75063, as two-sided custom fabricated, internally illuminated aluminum pylon signs with backlighted LED construction, power at 120 V, 60 Hz, 1 phase, 15 A, weep holes, computer cut panels with push through white acrylic lettering, and a box depth of 1'-6". Aluminum panels meet ASTM B209, alloy EN 5052 H12, minimum 0.05 inch (1.25mm) thick; extrusions meet ASTM B221, alloy 6063-T5. Finishes are a two-phase high temperature cured polyester color coating with a 2 mil thick chromium primer layer and a two-component, water-based, non-toxic, lead-free, zero emissions top coat, with LTV series die cut vinyl or surface screen process graphics.

LED message centers use a basis of design of Thinksign Model Xtreme V-2 16 mm display, or Daktronics, Spectrum, or approved equal. New display housing dimensions are approximately 3'-8" tall by 7'-4" wide and retrofit housings approximately 4'-2" tall by 7'-4" wide, with front-to-back depth not exceeding 7 inches. Maximum display power shall not exceed 1000 watts at full drive current; displays operate from 120/240 VAC, 60 Hz single-phase, in ambient temperatures of -40 to +120 degrees F and 95% humidity. The full LED matrix measures a minimum of 60 pixel rows high by 150 pixel columns wide, full color, 16mm pitch, 4.4 inch character height, pixel configuration of 1 red, 1 green and 1 blue, with modules and power supplies fully encapsulated and sealed to IP-67 standards, no less than a 140 degree horizontal half-intensity viewing angle and 160 degree horizontal readability angle. Controllers run independently of a controlling computer, connect to light and temperature sensors, store presentations and schedules in non-volatile memory, and include a 4G or 5G lifetime cellular communications package with the manufacturer's latest LED message center software.

Materials and installation. Steel materials include ASTM A653/A653M sheet, ASTM A36/A36M or A529/A529M shapes, ASTM A529/A529M or A572/A572M plate or bar stock at 42,000-psi minimum yield strength, ASTM A500/A500M Grade B tubing, and ASTM A307 or A325 bolts; acrylic sheet meets ASTM D4802 Type UVF, polycarbonate ASTM C1349 Appendix X1 Type II, bituminous paint ASTM D1187/D1187M, and nonshrink nonmetallic grout ASTM C1107/C1107M. Aluminum posts are 0.125-inch thick extruded tubing and steel posts minimum 0.120-inch thick tubing, hot-dip galvanized per ASTM A123/A123M; direct burial posts are fabricated 42 inches longer than the height of the sign. Posts and pylons are set plumb within a tolerance of 1/16 inch in 3 feet; unsuitable subgrade is excavated an additional 12 inches and backfilled in 6-inch compacted lifts; preformed holes in concrete foundations are not less than 3/4 inch larger than the outside dimension of the post. LED displays must be grounded per Article 250 of the National Electrical Code. The package closes with aerial location imagery credited to Maxar Technologies, U.S. Geological Survey and Google, dated 2020 with image capture September 2018, labeled 201 W Square Lake Rd and 4200 John R Rd.

**Other: Niles Center invest-or-divest analysis**
Rick West's July 15, 2019 memorandum to Dr. Rich Machesky quotes the Friday, June 28th Communique and estimates $1,300,000 to renovate Niles without demolition, $1,900,000 to renovate after removing the early childhood wing and adding 30 parking spaces, and $500,000 to demolish the building entirely; none include flooring or casework. **Schools of Choice, Section 105c.** Michigan law requires a resolution each school year from districts intending to participate; seats were anticipated for 2020-2021 in grade 9 at the International Academy East. The resolution, exercising the option permitted by Section 105c of the State School Aid Act of 1979 as amended by Public Act 300 of 1996, would accept applications from 85 non-resident 9th grade students residing outside Oakland County whose intermediate school district is contiguous with Oakland Intermediate School District boundaries.

**OCSBA legislative priorities.** Oakland County School Boards Association resolutions covering mental health (MASB Resolutions G 9.01, G 9.05, G 9.50), local control (A 10.10, A 10.55, A 12.70), evidence-based decision making (G 11.01), unfunded mandates (A 10.20), the School Finance Research Collaborative, school aid planks A through E (A 10.25 subsections, A 10.55, A 10.05), accountability and transparency (A 6.65), lame duck parameters, universal preschool for four year olds (A 6.15 (c)) and full funding of the federal Individuals with Disabilities Education Act, which initially promised 40 percent of excess cost (A 5.01; NSBA Advocacy: IDEA). Plank E asks that the annual School Aid Budget be enacted no later than June 1 so districts can meet the June 30 budget adoption requirement. The cover letter from Birgit McQuiston, Secretary of the OCSBA Board of Directors, sets a voting window of August 1 through September 15, requires approval by at least nineteen member school districts, and reports results at the September 24 OCSBA meeting; Resolutions and Bylaws Committee members are Carol Finkelstein (248-321-7999), Marc Katz and McQuiston.

**Personnel.** Superintendent Dr. Richard Machesky completed his fourth year as a highly effective superintendent and exceeded expectations in all evaluation categories, the item citing his support of oneTROY and Troy as a destination district on its journey to world class; the resolution extends his contract from July 1, 2019 through June 30, 2024 without tenure in the administrative position. Item 6.B covers Rick West (Business Services), Kris Griffor (Elementary Instruction) and Jordan Harris (Employee Services), whose contracts expire June 30, 2019; the text describes both one-year extensions and two-year successor contracts commencing July 1, 2019 and terminating June 30, 2021, without tenure.

**Meeting schedule and closed session.** The January 14, 2020 Organizational and Regular Meeting was inadvertently scheduled for the second Tuesday; the resolution moves it to January 21, 2020, consistent with third-Tuesday practice. The attached 2019 schedule lists regular meetings at the Services Building, 4420 Livernois, at 7:00 p.m. on January 15, February 26, March 19, April 16, May 21, June 4 (at Athens), July 16, August 20, September 17, October 15, November 19 and December 17, and workshops at the Administrative Center, 4400 Livernois, at 6:00 p.m. on January 8, February 5, March 5 (Troy Center for Transition), April 9, May 7, June 11, September 3, October 1, November 12, December 3 and January 7, 2020. The closed session resolution, as permitted in the Michigan Open Meetings Act, Public Act 267, Section 8 (c), would take the Board into closed session to discuss an attorney-client privilege by roll call vote of trustees Fleming, Gottlieb, Hammond, Hauff, Philippart, Schmidt and Wilson.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
Official minutes of the Board of Education, Troy, Michigan, for the board meeting of September 15, 2020, conducted as a Zoom Webinar. A public notice was posted in order to allow community members to participate remotely.

CALL TO ORDER AND ATTENDANCE. President Schmidt called the meeting to order at 7:05 p.m. In addition to Mr. Schmidt, present via Zoom videoconference were board members Anne, Gottlieb, Hammond, Hauff, Philippart and Wilson — a full seven-member board. Also present were Superintendent Machesky; administrators Birmingham, Carrier, Griffor, DiPilato, Pagel and West; and approximately 275 additional members of the audience.

RECOGNITION — ASBO CERTIFICATE OF EXCELLENCE. The Association of School Business Officials International's Certificate of Excellence in Financial Reporting Program honored the Troy School District for excellence in the preparation and issuance of a high quality Comprehensive Annual Financial Report (CAFR) for the fiscal year ended June 30, 2019. The minutes note that the Certificate of Excellence in Financial Reporting was created by ASBO International to enable business officials to achieve a high standard of financial reporting, and recognize Kandice Moynihan, Finance Director, and her staff for their effort and continued dedication to excellence.

STUDENT REPRESENTATIVES FOR BOARD MEETINGS. President Schmidt introduced and welcomed four high school student representatives to the Board for the 2020-2021 school year. Carlton Thomas of Troy College & Career High School, beginning his second year as a student representative, was not in attendance; the minutes describe him as a senior and one of TCCHS's strongest leaders academically and socially, devoted to his family, currently employed by the Troy School District as a student technology support technician, with post-secondary goals of obtaining a journeyman's license as an electrician and eventually owning his own electrical company. Pranay Gupta of International Academy-East, also in his second year as a representative, is a senior involved in the school's robotics team, Forensics club, and the school's symphony and full orchestras, and plans to pursue engineering and business in college. Nathania Nartey is a senior and a Redhawk at Athens High School, an all-A honors and Summa Cum Laude student who competes on the varsity track and cheer teams and values the sense of community sports provide and Athens' community-outreach opportunities. Sejal Patil is a senior at Troy High School active in Troy High's HOSA chapter and Student Government and founder of a club called Connect4Cancer; she plans to become a surgical oncologist and lists photography, piano, biking and helping her community among her hobbies.

REPORTS FROM STUDENT REPRESENTATIVES. Pranay Gupta shared a brief update on how the school year had started, noting the International Academy-East had been in school for 19 days. Nathania Nartey shared a brief update on how the virtual learning platform was going at Athens High School, and Sejal Patil did the same for Troy High School. Carlton Thomas was not present.

NATIONAL SCHOOL OF CHARACTER AWARD. The Board honored Wass and Wattles Elementary Schools for receiving the 2020 National School of Character Award. Wass and Wattles were two of 84 schools across the country to receive the distinction from Character.org, a national advocate and leader for character in education. The program recognized the schools for using character development to drive a positive impact on academics, student behavior and cultural climate. Under the leadership of Principals Matt Jansen and Dr. Joyce Brasington, the committee praised the schools for promoting good character, culture and ethics; fostering student self-motivation; giving students the opportunity for moral action; and engaging families and community members as partners in character-building efforts. Mr. Jansen invited Wass teacher Mark Cavataio to speak on behalf of Wass Elementary, and Dr. Brasington shared remarks about the Wattles staff.

ADDITIONS AND DELETIONS. None.

PUBLIC COMMUNICATION (AGENDA ITEMS). Troy resident Troy Otto addressed the Board regarding in-person learning for students. Troy resident Matthew Sims addressed the Board regarding a safe and effective return to in-person education. Troy resident Rebecca Anders addressed the Board regarding in-person instruction for students with IEPs. Troy resident Stacey Olsen addressed the Board in support of virtual schooling for Troy students.

GENERAL — CONSENT AGENDA (RESOLUTION 20-072). It was moved by Mr. Hauff and supported by Mrs. Anne that the Troy Board of Education approve items A, B, C and D on the consent agenda: minutes of the August 5, 2020 Special Board of Education Workshop; minutes of the August 12, 2020 Special Board of Education Meeting; minutes of the August 18, 2020 Special Board of Education Meeting; and the Treasurer's Report for July 2020. On a roll call vote, Wilson, Anne, Gottlieb, Hammond, Hauff, Philippart and Schmidt all voted yes: 7 yes, 0 no.

PERSONNEL — ELEMENTARY AND SECONDARY (RESOLUTION 20-073). It was moved by Mrs. Hammond and supported by Dr. Philippart that the Board approve the personnel recommendations. The new hires listed are Jordan Moses, Jaynie Sorenson, Rachel Cervi, Katelyn Bowman, Megan Feeley, Eric Kravako, Kasey Garvelink, Erica Peplinski, M. Katherine Allen, Morgan Clark, Alexander Welsh, Shelby Allard, Kristina Forbes, Lauren Church, Katelyn Atkinson, Rachel Scott, Madison Hileman and Andre Gilford. On a roll call vote, Anne, Gottlieb, Hammond, Hauff, Philippart, Schmidt and Wilson voted yes: 7 yes, 0 no.

STAFFING UPDATE. John Pagel, Director of Employee Services, provided a brief update on teacher staffing for the 2020/2021 school year and described the factors influencing the number of teachers hired, including retirements and resignations, full-year leaves of absence, FTE status, and student enrollment.

CURRICULUM — EQUITY UPDATE. Kris Griffor, Assistant Superintendent for Elementary Instruction, and Christine DiPilato, Assistant Superintendent for Secondary Instruction, shared a PowerPoint presentation on the equity and inclusion work happening in the District and the professional learning staff are participating in. They discussed the district's continued and expanded partnership with the National Equity Project and the hosting of community conversations with students, staff and families. Board discussion followed the presentation.

ENROLLMENT UPDATE. Kris Griffor provided an update on the District's enrollment status, thanked the Central Enrollment team for their work enrolling the many new families who had joined the District, and reported enrollment numbers as of that day while noting the numbers were still changing daily.

BUSINESS — PURCHASE OF PPE (RESOLUTION 20-074). It was moved by Dr. Wilson and supported by Dr. Philippart that the district purchase acrylic shields from IMBranded in the amount of $445,387.90 and that this amount be approved as an expenditure of the General Fund. On a roll call vote, Gottlieb, Hammond, Hauff, Philippart, Schmidt, Wilson and Anne voted yes: 7 yes, 0 no.

BOND, BUILDING AND SITE SINKING FUND UPDATE. Mr. West, Assistant Superintendent of Business Services, and Rob Carson, Director of Maintenance & Operations, provided an update on building improvement projects, the Niles relocation project, and the renovation of the Troy School District Learning Center, sharing a PowerPoint with slides of site improvement projects at various schools throughout the District. Beth Soggs, Director of Technology, provided an update on technology bond projects completed over the summer, including upgrades to AV systems, additional security cameras and iPads.

OTHER — SUPERINTENDENT'S UPDATE. Dr. Machesky, Superintendent, shared a PowerPoint presentation providing an update on the District's Return to Learn Plan.

PUBLIC COMMUNICATION (NON-AGENDA ITEMS). None. Mr. Schmidt announced that the next Board Workshop would be held Tuesday, October 6 at 6:00 p.m. and the next regular Board Meeting on October 20 at 7:00 p.m.

CLOSED SESSION — NEGOTIATIONS. It was moved by Mrs. Anne and supported by Dr. Philippart that, as permitted in the Michigan Open Meetings Act, Public Act 267, Section 8(c), the Troy Board of Education go into closed session to discuss negotiations. On a roll call vote, Hammond, Hauff, Philippart, Schmidt, Wilson, Anne and Gottlieb voted yes: 7 yes, 0 no. The Board moved into closed session at 10:08 p.m. and the meeting reconvened at 10:09 p.m.

ADJOURNMENT. The meeting adjourned at 10:53 p.m. The minutes are respectfully submitted by Gary N. Hauff, Secretary, Troy Board of Education, with the typist notation GH/jh.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.paragraph: Board presentation titled "What is a Board Member?" prepared for the October 20, 2020 Troy Board of Education meeting, laying out the legal and ethical framework governing individual school board members and then applying it to a specific case. After reviewing the Michigan School Code, the National School Boards Association Code of Ethics, Michigan Association of School Boards governance standards and the district's own Code of Ethics in Policy Manual Section 1000.01, the deck presents the case for disclaiming and censuring Trustee Elizabeth Hammond over Facebook posts to a Troy Parent Group on September 23 and 24, 2020. It closes with a motion by Nancy Philippart declaring that Trustee Hammond's opinions and actions are those of an individual community member and do not represent the Troy Board of Education.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.page:
**Purpose**
A governance presentation to the Troy Board of Education on the role and limits of an individual school board member, followed by the case for disclaiming and censuring Trustee Elizabeth Hammond.

**Governance framework**
School board members are elected officials who must uphold the Michigan Constitution's mandate to provide free public elementary and secondary education. Under the School Code, board powers include actions incidental or appropriate to operating the district and in the interests of public elementary and secondary education; educating pupils K-12, preschool and adult education; providing for the safety and welfare of students; acquiring and disposing of school property; matters involving the receipt and expenditure of school funds; and joint agreements and cooperative arrangements — but actions cannot conflict with or circumvent state prohibitions.

**Ethical standards cited**
- National School Boards Association Code of Ethics: "As a member of my local Board of Education I will strive to improve public education, and to that end I will take no private action that will compromise the board or administration."
- Michigan Association of School Boards Board of Education Governance Standards, endorsed by the Michigan State Board of Education, standards 3.a (no independent legal authority for individual members), 3.c (follows established policies and procedures), 3.d (supports decisions of the Board after a vote regardless of individual position), and 3.g (understanding of and respect for district structure and protocols).
- TSD Policy Manual Section 1000.01, Organization and Functioning of the Board: each member has signed a Code of Ethics acknowledging no individual legal authority, decisions only by majority vote at a public meeting, no private action compromising the Board or administration, respect for confidentiality of privileged information, abiding by majority decisions, and a positive working relationship with the Superintendent.

**Remedies for violations**
Censure is defined via Oxford Languages as the expressing of "formal disapproval"; by majority vote the Board may censure a member for violating federal or Michigan law, the Bylaws or Board policy. Separately, Michigan law requires a board to act only as a board; under Section 1201 of the Revised School Code trustees may exercise power only collectively at a regular or properly called special meeting. A disclaiming motion passed by a board majority alerts the community that an individual trustee's actions do not represent the will of the board.

**Prior counsel to Trustee Hammond**
The deck states she was informally advised on at least three occasions: the President's letter of October 2, 2019; the Board self evaluation of January 2020; and the special board meeting of September 29, 2020.

**Posts at issue**
Four Facebook exchanges in the Troy Parent Group are quoted: a September 23, 2020 post asserting the current plan "DOES NOT" adhere to safety protocols and "PUTS THE ENTIRE COMMUNITY AT RISK"; a September 24, 2020 exchange about the 4 p.m. timing of the September 29 special board meeting ("unfortunately I couldn't control the time"); a September 24 reply about face shields ("We are so screwed. Thank you for being so vocal."); and a September 24 post describing pulled special education small groups as "a potential SUPER SPREADER."

**District responses**
The Return to Learn plan was approved by the county and state and developed with epidemiologists, nurses and public health leaders at the Oakland County Health Division, and meets all state-mandated safety measures while exceeding many recommended protocols — masks Pre K-12, elementary cohorting and reduced secondary class changes, seating charts, staggered passing times, plexiglass barriers, additional PPE, limits on guests, mandatory health screening, attendance policy changes, enhanced cleaning, OCHD nurse walkthroughs and dedicated building nurses. Special education protocols include mandatory handwashing, assigned seats and distancing, open classroom doors, no more than three students in a room at once, and wipe-down of work areas. Special meetings are scheduled around board member availability via a timing poll to which Trustee Hammond responded without requesting additional times, and meetings are streamed on Zoom or, when more than 1,000 people attend, to Facebook and YouTube.

**Labor exposure**
A September 24, 2020 letter from the Troy Education Association asserts that a board member discussing plan specifics with individual members outside collective bargaining is an unfair labor practice under PERA; the deck notes Trustee Hammond is the only board member active on social media and warns a PERA complaint could lead to a lawsuit and financial damages.

**Motion**
Nancy Philippart moves that the actions of Trustee Hammond are not the actions of the Troy Board of Education and that the community be alerted that, unless specifically authorized by motion of the board, Trustee Hammond's opinions and actions are as an individual community member.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
Presentation titled "WHAT IS A BOARD MEMBER?" delivered to the Troy Board of Education on October 20, 2020. It begins as a primer on school board governance and ethics and concludes as the formal case for disclaiming and censuring Trustee Elizabeth Hammond.

GOVERNANCE. The deck establishes that school board members are elected officials who must uphold the Michigan Constitution's mandate to provide free public elementary and secondary education. Under the School Code, the general powers a Board of Education may execute include actions incidental or appropriate to the performance of a function related to the operation of the district; actions in the interests of public elementary and secondary education; educating pupils in K-12, preschool and adult education; providing for the safety and welfare of students; acquiring and disposing of school property; matters involving the receipt and expenditure of school funds; and joint agreements and cooperative arrangements. The slide adds the qualification that actions cannot conflict with or circumvent state prohibitions.

HOW SCHOOL BOARDS WORK. Two external standards are quoted. The National School Boards Association Code of Ethics for School Board Members provides: "As a member of my local Board of Education I will strive to improve public education, and to that end I will take no private action that will compromise the board or administration." The Michigan Association of School Boards Board of Education Governance Standards, endorsed by the Michigan State Board of Education, state that the individual school board member understands and respects both the authority and responsibilities of the Board of Education, and the deck cites four sub-standards: 3.a, the board member acts in accordance with Michigan law, which does not vest individual board members with any type of independent legal authority; 3.c, the board member follows established policies and procedures; 3.d, the board member supports decisions of the Board of Education after a vote is taken regardless of his or her individual position prior to the vote; and 3.g, the board member demonstrates understanding of and respect for school district structure and protocols.

HOW WE DO THIS IN THE TROY SCHOOL DISTRICT. The district's own Code of Ethics is set out in TSD Policy Manual Section 1000.01, Organization and Functioning of the Board. Each Board member has acknowledged and signed an excerpt providing that as a member of the Board he or she will promote the best interest of the School District as a whole and adhere to stated ethical standards and principles: recognizing that a Board member has no legal authority as an individual and that decisions can be made only by a majority vote at a public meeting of the Board; taking no private action that might compromise the Board or administration and respecting the confidentiality of privileged information; abiding by majority decisions of the Board while retaining the right to seek changes through ethical and constructive channels; and striving for a positive working relationship with the Superintendent, respecting the Superintendent's authority to advise the Board, implement Board policy, and administer the School District.

WHAT ABOUT VIOLATIONS — CENSURE. Citing Oxford Languages, censure is defined as the expressing of "formal disapproval." The quoted bylaw language provides that by a majority vote, the Board may censure an individual Board member or members for violating federal or Michigan law, these Bylaws or Board policy, or otherwise acting in a manner inconsistent with the office of a Board member.

DISCLAIMING ACTS OF INDIVIDUAL BOARD MEMBERS. Michigan law requires that a school board act only as a board, not as private individuals, and only the vote of a majority of a board's members creates action by the board. Under Section 1201 of the Revised School Code, trustees may only exercise power and perform their duties as trustees when doing so collectively and only at a regular or a properly called special meeting. When a trustee violates this law and fellow board members are concerned that the community may misconstrue the trustee's individual actions as representative of the board, they may disclaim the actions of that trustee; a disclaiming motion passed by the majority alerts the community that the actions of an individual trustee do not represent the will of the board.

ETHICS VIOLATIONS — TRUSTEE ELIZABETH HAMMOND. The deck states that the decision to publicly discuss the case for disclaiming and censure of Trustee Hammond did not come lightly, and that the violations of ethics and state law to be shared are not isolated instances over a short timeframe but a repeated pattern of behavior. It records that Trustee Hammond was informally advised on at least three different occasions to address behaviors violating the ethics of her role as trustee: the President's letter of October 2, 2019; the Board self evaluation of January 2020; and the special board meeting of September 29, 2020. Her response, the deck asserts, was to disregard this advice, leaving no recourse but to bring the discussion forward.

POST OF WEDNESDAY, SEPTEMBER 23, 2020. Quoted from the Troy Parent Group: "My position has always been that I support the parents' right to make a choice for their own families while we are in, what the governor defines as, Phase 4. That said, I do NOT believe that an in-person option should throw science out the window. A safely executed in-person option requires strict adherence to both required and recommended safety protocols. THE CURRENT PLAN DOES NOT DO THIS AND PUTS THE ENTIRE COMMUNITY AT RISK. Further, I believe the current scenario leaves those students who choose to remain at home, at both an educational and social disadvantage. It also makes highly effective teaching virtually impossible (no pun intended)." The response slide calls the post inaccurate, inflammatory and a creator of unnecessary fear and apprehension: the TSD Return to Learn plan does not throw science out the window nor put the entire community at risk; the plan was approved by the county and state and developed with epidemiologists, nurses and public health leaders at the Oakland County Health Division; and it meets all state-mandated safety measures while exceeding many recommended protocols, including requiring masks Pre K-12; cohorting students in elementary school and reduced class changes at secondary; seating charts in classrooms, lunchrooms and segregated playground areas by class; staggered passing time and enhanced safety procedures for building entry, recess and dismissal; plexiglass barriers between teachers and students; additional PPE such as face shields, gowns and gloves used in conjunction with masks; significantly limiting guests in buildings; mandatory health screening of all students, staff, vendors and contractors; attendance policy changes; enhanced cleaning protocols; walkthroughs in every building with OCHD nurses for guidance on sick rooms and other operational issues; dedicated nurses assigned to each building; and strict protocols for food distribution in cafeterias. The impact slide argues the post harms trust between the public, school community and district/board at a time when trust is critical, and insinuates the District is deliberately withholding information.

POST OF THURSDAY, SEPTEMBER 24, 2020 — MEETING TIME. A parent wrote of the September 29 special board meeting, "I feel they make it on 4pm on purpose because most of the parents are working at that time," to which Elizabeth Hammond replied, "I have the same concern.... unfortunately I couldn't control the time." The response states the post is inaccurate and does not reflect the need to manage around board members' schedules: special meetings are scheduled quickly and sometimes begin earlier than the normal 6 or 7 p.m. time to ensure board members can participate, with priority given to board members' availability based on responses to a timing poll; Trustee Hammond responded to the poll and did not request additional times be added. All meetings and workshops are streamed via Zoom, or when more than 1,000 people attend, streamed to Facebook and YouTube, and recordings are available. The impact slide argues the post insinuates the district is intentionally avoiding public participation and that her statement "I couldn't control the time" reflects a lack of ownership that erodes trust.

POST OF THURSDAY, SEPTEMBER 24, 2020 — FACE SHIELDS. A parent wrote, "I read today that due to the aerosol nature of the virus the face shields are actually ineffective at stopping the spread. No idea if this extends to plexiglass dividers." Elizabeth Hammond replied, "[PARENT NAME] right??? We are so screwed. Thank you for being so vocal." The response states the safety plan calls for multiple mitigation measures used together and does not rely on any single protocol; face shields are used in conjunction with masks with rare exceptions, such as a student with significant needs who cannot tolerate a cloth mask; and plexiglass shields are used in conjunction with physical distancing, signage, handwashing, other hygiene measures and strict policies for illness and health screening. The impact slide argues that Trustee Hammond had been present for hours of discussion on mitigation measures, that telling a community member "we are so screwed" rather than discussing facts and risks is intentionally inflammatory, and that "thanks for being so vocal" suggests she is creating fear to build support for her own personal choices as a parent, making a case for negligent behavior on the part of the board and district administration.

POST OF THURSDAY, SEPTEMBER 24, 2020 — LUNCH AND SPECIAL EDUCATION. Quoted: "From everything I read, it sounds like multiple classrooms will be in the cafeteria at the same time eating without masks! Also, for SE services, in most cases small groups would be pulled from multiple classes and spend a couple hours a week together. They would be with a SE teacher that would cover all classes in multiple grades — a potential SUPER SPREADER." The response notes she had been part of multiple discussions on lunch and support-service protocols. For lunch, additional locations such as art rooms, gyms and LGI rooms are used to keep classes isolated; in the cafeteria classes are distanced at least six feet from one another and individual classes are seated according to seating charts; photos posted on social media indicate that in most cases individual students are six feet or more apart when masks come off; and elementary schools have segregated areas of the playground, fields and blacktop with a rotating schedule so cohorts do not mix. For special education support services, protocols include mandatory hand washing before entering the interventionist's room and before returning to the general education classroom; assigned seats and physical distancing; classroom doors left open to ensure air flow; no more than three students in the room at one time; students wiping down their work area on arrival; masks for students and staff with additional PPE for teachers such as face shields, desktop and mobile plexiglass dividers, gloves and hand sanitizer; and mandatory daily health screenings with strong encouragement to stay home when sick. The impact slide states that referring to special education students and staff as "potential SUPER SPREADERS" is demeaning and unfair and potentially harms the integration of these students into general education classrooms.

TROY EDUCATION ASSOCIATION LETTER, SEPTEMBER 24, 2020. The excerpt reads: "The public communications on social media, the discussion of permissible bargaining issues, and the positional statements that run counter to the efforts of our collective teams, must stop. It is the position of the Association that any dialog with individual members of the Troy Education Association about decisions made by the Board and Central Administration on virtual learning or hybrid learning scenarios is an unfair labor practice. The Troy Education Association selects a bargaining team to represent the interests of all members. The Association contends that a board member discussing the specifics of the plan with individual members outside of the collective bargaining process is detrimental and a blatant attempt to undermine the rights afforded to the Association under the guidelines proscribed through PERA." The response notes that although individuals were not specifically named, Trustee Hammond is the only board member active on social media, and her social media behavior is being construed by the association as public negotiation and thus an unfair labor practice under the Public Employment Relations Act. The stated impact is that a PERA complaint could potentially lead to a lawsuit and financial damages to the district.

CASE FOR DISCLAIMING/CENSURE. The summary slide holds that Trustee Hammond committed to "take no private action that will compromise the board or administration" yet her social media posts presented inaccurate and inflammatory information harming trust between the District, its staff, students and community; insinuated that the District is intentionally avoiding public participation; potentially created bias regarding special education staff and students; and insinuated that the board and administration are negligent in their attention to student and staff safety. It further holds that she committed to "act in accordance with Michigan law" yet her posts are being construed as PERA violations by the Troy Education Association, and that she committed to "support decisions of the Board of Education after vote regardless of her individual position prior to vote" yet the letter of complaint from the Troy Education Association President and the dates of her social media posts show she continued to undermine board decisions made on Return to Learn plans on August 12.

MOTION TO DISCLAIM ACTS OF AN INDIVIDUAL BOARD MEMBER. The closing slides restate that Michigan law requires the board to act collectively and not let actions as private individuals compromise the board or District and its relationship with the community; that given the social media posts by Trustee Hammond, who is seen as a representative of the board, the community's interpretation of recent actions may be misconstrued to represent those of the board and District; and that a disclaiming motion is being made to alert the community that Trustee Hammond's actions do not represent, nor are authorized by, the Troy Board of Education. The motion as drafted reads: "I, Nancy Philippart move that the actions of Trustee Hammond are not the actions of the Troy Board of Education and that the community and its members be alerted that unless specifically authorized by motion of this board, Trustee Hammond opinions and actions are as an individual community member and should not be construed as representing the Troy Board of Education."

**Organizational business.** The prior year's president opens; Judy Holmes is appointed temporary secretary; president, vice president and secretary are elected to serve until December 31, 2020, with four votes required, roll call rotating among Philippart, Schmidt, Wilson, Fleming, Gottlieb, Hauff and Hammond. Rick West, Assistant Superintendent, Business Services, is appointed Treasurer for January through December 2020 as a nonvoting officer.

The fund depository and investment resolution designates Bank of America, Charter One Bank, JP Morgan Chase Bank, Comerica Bank, Huntington Bank, Fifth Third Bank, Flagstar Bancorp, MILAF (Michigan Liquid Asset Fund Plus, managed by PFM Asset Management, Inc. through Fifth Third Bank), Morgan Stanley Smith Barney, PFM Securities, Inc. through Fifth Third Bank, and PNC Bank. Checks carry Rick West's facsimile signature; in emergencies West or Superintendent Machesky may hand-sign on the Bank of America General Fund and Payroll accounts. PNC Bank accounts pay Troy Career Center expenses; a Comerica Bank account pays flexible spending claims by ACH debit to Next Generation Enrollment, Inc. Investments follow Board Policy 5000.06, and the Treasurer may combine money from more than one fund under subsection (1)(h) of Section 380.1223 of the Revised School Code. Legal counsel for calendar 2020: Clark Hill, PLC; Collins & Blaha, P.C.; Lusk Albertson; Thrun Law Firm, P.C.; and Beier Howlett, P.C. The Superintendent continues as Deputy Secretary and Judy Holmes as the person posting meeting notices. Regular meetings are set for February 25, March 17, April 21, May 19, June 2 (at Athens), June 16, July 21, August 18, September 15, October 20, November 17 and December 15, 2020, and January 19, 2021, with a Saturday, March 7, 2020 Winter Retreat among the 6:00 p.m. workshops.

**Recognitions.** Adam Burns, Technology Education/English teacher at Athens High School, and Athens TV students Ellen Bedford, Abby Bright, Grace Bright, Grace Joo and Madison Strachan are recognized for the Michigan Arctic Grayling Initiative; Kris Griffor, Assistant Superintendent, Elementary Instruction, for the 2020 National Excellence in Literacy Leadership Award from Reading Recovery Teacher Leaders; and Paula Fleming, retiring after more than 19 years and moving to Arkansas, with proclamations from Mayor Ethan Baker and State Representative Padma Kuppa.

**Consent agenda minutes.** Items A-G cover the corrected November 12, 2019 workshop (David Hulings, motivational leadership coach), the December 3, 2019 workshop (Philippart absent; Paul Wills of Plante Moran; Plante Moran CRESA enrollment update), the December 17, 2019 special meeting (Fleming and Gottlieb absent; Section 1 to be rebid with an RFP after the first of the year; Resolution 19-095 closed session under the Michigan Open Meetings Act, PA 267, Section 8(c), with Hammond, Hauff, Philippart, Schmidt and Wilson voting yes), the closed session, the December 17 regular meeting and a special workshop. **Meeting**
Troy School District Board of Education, Special Meeting (virtual/remote), April 14, 2020, 5:45 PM, on Zoom, Meeting ID 248 952 1600, dial-in 253-215-8782 or 301-715-8592. Adjournment. Both items carry roll-call votes naming Gottlieb, Hammond, Hauff, Philippart, Schmidt, Wilson and Anne.

**TEA contract ratification (item 3.A)**
Tentative agreement with the Troy Education Association/MEA/NEA was reached March 27, 2020 and ratified by TEA membership April 2, 2020, covering February 1, 2020 through January 31, 2021. The agreement is executed "this 14th day of April 2020"; TEA offices are at 17500 West 11 Mile, Ste. 200, Lathrup Village, MI 48076. Article 39 directs both teams to meet on or before October 15, 2020 about negotiations.

**Economic terms (Article 11.1)**
As of May 1st, eligible teachers on Steps 2 through 13 receive a lump sum equal to half their current step increment and move a half step. As of May 15th, teachers who began 2019-2020 on Longevity 1, 2 or 3 receive $500.00 and all teachers receive a $200.00 ratification bonus. As of July 1, 2020 eligible teachers move one step and each cell of Schedule A (Steps 1 through 14) increases by $500.00, with a $500.00 off-schedule payment in the first pay period of 2020-2021.

**Schedule A, 2020-2021 (selected)**

| Step | BA | MA | MA30/EDS/ESL | PHD/EDD |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 41,800 | 45,500 | 48,700 | 52,000 |
| 7 | 56,200 | 63,500 | 69,100 | 72,400 |
| 14 | 73,500 | 85,000 | 93,400 | 96,700 |

BA-lane longevity increments are 2,682, 4,564 and 6,445, for service beyond 15, 20 and 25 years. Schedules B and C pay a percentage of $64,000 (raised from $60,467) — varsity football and basketball 11.60% ($7,424.00). Schedule D pays $30.00 per hour for curriculum development.

**Minimum Fund Balance**
A minimum fund balance of 12% is defined as the audited General Fund Equity balance of at least 12% of the 2017-2018 and 2018-2019 fiscal year total expenditures per each June 30 audit. Any shortfall measured at November 30, 2018 and/or November 30, 2019 is the "Deficiency"; multiplied by 55.6% it becomes the "Contribution," an equal-percentage off-schedule reduction of base salaries. A balance above 17% yields a "Surplus"; multiplied by 55.6% it becomes the "Bonus," paid in the second payroll in March 2019 and/or March 2020. Capital asset sale proceeds over $2 million are excluded.

**COVID-19 policy (item 4.A)**
Adopted in accordance with Executive Order 2020-35, with the first reading waived under policy 1000.03. Employees testing positive or showing principal symptoms (fever, atypical cough, atypical shortness of breath) may not enter district property until three days after symptoms resolve and seven days after they first appear or since swabbing, or upon a negative test; close contact within approximately six feet requires 14 days. Executive Order 2020-36 bars retaliation. FFCRA emergency paid sick leave provides up to 80 hours capped at $511 per day and $5,110 in the aggregate for an employee's own quarantine, and $200 per day and $2,000 in the aggregate for care of others. Emergency FMLA expansion gives up to 12 weeks for care of a child under 18, capped at $200 per day and $10,000 in the aggregate. The policy expires December 31, 2020.
