Roll-call lines name Gottlieb, Hammond, Hauff, Philippart, Schmidt, Wilson and Anne.

ITEM 3.A — TEA CONTRACT RATIFICATION (dated 04.14.20). Board representatives and the Troy Education Association/MEA/NEA reached a tentative agreement March 27, 2020; TEA membership ratified it April 2, 2020. The contract period is February 1, 2020 through January 31, 2021. The attached agreement is between the Troy Education Association, a local affiliate of MEA/NEA (17500 West 11 Mile, Ste. 200, Lathrup Village, MI 48076) and the Troy School District Board of Education, executed "this 14th day of April 2020," with signature blocks for the Board President and Superintendent and the TEA President and Secretary. The redlined Table of Contents places Article 37 Ancillary Teachers at page 62, Article 38 Minimum Fund Balance at page 78 and Article 39 Duration of Agreement at page 80, which directs both teams to meet on or before October 15, 2020 to discuss negotiations.

SALARY SETTLEMENT (Article 11.1). As of May 1st, eligible teachers on Steps 2 through 13, and those who moved to Step 13.5 during 2019-2020, receive a lump sum equal to half their current step increment and move a half step. As of May 15th, eligible teachers who began 2019-2020 on Longevity 1, 2 or 3 receive $500.00, added to the 2020-2021 Schedule A longevity steps, and all teachers receive a $200.00 ratification bonus. As of July 1, 2020 all eligible teachers move one salary step and each cell of Schedule A (Steps 1 through 14) increases by $500.00; a $500.00 off-schedule payment is made in the first pay period of 2020-2021. Teachers elect 21 or 26 equal payments. Six paid holidays are observed: Labor Day, Thanksgiving Day, Christmas Day, New Year's Day, Good Friday and Memorial Day.

SCHEDULE A, 2020-2021. Eleven lanes are printed — BA, BA20, MA, MA30/EDS/ESL Endorsement, PHD/EDD, and grandfathered BA25, MA5, MA10, MA15, MA20 and MA25. Step 1 pays 41,800 (BA), 45,500 (MA), 48,700 (MA30/EDS) and 52,000 (PHD/EDD); Step 14 pays 73,500, 85,000, 93,400 and 96,700, topping out at 91,750 in MA25. Longevity increments run 2,682 / 4,564 / 6,445 in the BA lane and 3,269 / 5,734 / 8,204 in PHD/EDD, paid for service beyond 15, 20 and 25 years in Troy Schools. Teachers were barred from BA+15, BA+25, MA+5, MA+15 and MA+25 after 1996-97 and from MA+10 and MA+20 after 2009-10; only teachers hired on or before December 14, 1971 may advance to BA+30.

EXTRA-DUTY SCHEDULES. Schedules B and C pay a percentage of $64,000, raised from $60,467. Varsity football and basketball pay 11.60% ($7,424.00); assistant varsity and junior varsity 7.50% ($4,800.00); varsity gymnastics, wrestling, swimming and competitive cheer 9.00% ($5,760.00); varsity baseball, track, soccer, volleyball, lacrosse and hockey 8.00% ($5,120.00); varsity tennis, golf and cross country 6.00% ($3,840.00). Schedule C spans 7.50% ($4,800) for K-12 arts coordinators and the high school band director down to 1.00% ($640) club sponsorships. Schedule D pays $30.00 per hour for curriculum development, teaching in place of a substitute and TEAM/SAT meetings, $35.00 per hour plus a $60.00 annual prep fee for instructional trainers, and $20.00 per hour for web design, with mileage at the prevailing IRS maximum rate.

CLASS SIZE, STIPENDS AND SEVERANCE. Elementary maximums are 26 in kindergarten (27), 28 in first and second grade (30) and 29 in third through fifth (30), with $80 per marking period per student over the cap paid to the TEA Education Fund. Secondary base maximum is 30, with Advanced Placement at 25 (30), Progressive Learning Support at 21 (23), physical education at 33 in middle school and 36 in high school, and counselor caseload at 400 with $500 per semester if caseload exceeds 25 after count day; exceeding a maximum by one pupil in an emergency costs $1,000.00 per occurrence. Other stipends include $500 per year for secondary teachers traveling between schools, $350 per semester for early/late building assignments and $500 per mentee. Severance pays tenure teachers with ten or more years half the per diem rate for unused sick days to a maximum of 60 days plus 30 days at the substitute rate, and those with less than ten years the substitute rate to a maximum of 90 days; payments of $5,000.00 or more go into a District 403(b). Retirement severance pays $1,000.00 at 10-14 years, $1,500.00 at 15-19 years and $100.00 per year at 20 or more.

INSURANCE AND EARLY CHILDHOOD EDUCATORS. Article 26 maintains compliance with the Publicly Funded Health Insurance Contribution Act (PA 152 of 2011), the Board paying the annual maximum allowable and teachers the difference over 21 pays. MESSA PAK A bundles medical, Delta Dental, VSP III vision, life and long-term disability; life is two times salary, except $50,000 AD/D for teachers hired on or after June 4, 1991. Long-term disability begins after 60 calendar days and pays up to two-thirds of salary to age 70. Plan B pays $1,000 annually, or $2,500 if 45 or more teachers decline district medical coverage. New Article 36 covers early childhood educators in the Board's tuition-based preschool program under Michigan's Licensing and Regulatory Affairs (LARA), with a salary schedule of $28,008, $29,564, $31,120, $32,676 and $34,232 for Steps 1 through 5, a $1,000 annual master's stipend, a $3,000 cafeteria plan in lieu of medical coverage, a $50,000 term life policy and disability capped at $3,000 per month. Appendix 5 lists BCBSM plans CB 2, CB 3, CB 4 and Simply Blue effective 1/1/2020 with in-network deductibles of $100, $250, $500 and $1,400, and dental under Group #9941.

MINIMUM FUND BALANCE. The article sets a minimum fund balance of 12%, defined as the audited General Fund Equity balance of at least 12% of the 2017-2018 and 2018-2019 school/fiscal year total expenditures determined by each June 30 audit. If that balance falls below 12%, the amount needed to restore it is calculated as of November 30, 2018 and/or November 30, 2019 as the "Deficiency"; the Deficiency multiplied by 55.6% is the "Contribution," achieved by reducing base salaries of all actively employed bargaining unit members by an equal percentage through an off-schedule reduction beginning with the first payroll period in January 2018, accounting for retirement and FICA, unless another method is agreed before December 31, 2018 and/or December 31, 2019. Where the balance exceeds 17%, the excess measured on the same dates is the "Surplus"; the Surplus multiplied by 55.6% is the "Bonus," paid as an equal-percentage off-schedule lump sum in the second payroll in March 2019 and/or March 2020. Costs of new programs in excess of $2 million should not increase total year-over-year budgetary expenditures unless federally or state mandated, and one-time revenues from capital asset sales in excess of $2 million are excluded. Article 25.2 entitles the TEA to monthly financial reports.

CALENDARS AND APPENDICES. The 2020/2021 calendar totals 186 teacher days and 181 student days, with 6-12 marking periods ending November 5, January 21, March 25 and June 16. The payroll schedule runs from 8/21/2020 through 8/20/2021. A Letter of Agreement on Schoology grading amends Sections 14.14 and 14.15 of the 2017-2020 agreement through June 16, 2020. Appendix 1 is the grievance report form (rev/10-96), Appendix 2 the mentoring log, Appendix 3 board policies 4000.03 and 4000.04, and Appendix 4 the Child Care Supervisor Evaluation.

ITEM 4.A — COVID-19 BOARD POLICY. The Board considered a policy on COVID-19 Mitigation, Self-Reporting, Leave of Absence, noting that policy 1000.03 Adoption or Amendment of Bylaws and Policies permits waiver of a first reading. Adopted in accordance with Executive Order 2020-35, it bars employees and contractors who test positive or display principal symptoms from entering district property until three days have passed since symptoms resolved and seven days since symptoms first appeared or since swabbing, or until a negative test; close contact requires 14 days. Principal symptoms are fever, atypical cough or atypical shortness of breath; close contact is being within approximately six feet of an individual for a prolonged period. Executive Order 2020-36 prohibits retaliation for staying home. Employees must maintain at least six feet of distance and follow Centers for Disease Control and Prevention guidance; health information is protected under the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act of 1996 and the Family Education Rights and Privacy Act of 1974, with exposure reporting under Board Policy 5502. Under the FFCRA Emergency Paid Sick Leave Act, full-time employees receive up to 80 hours and part-time employees hours equal to their 2-week average, capped at $511 per day and $5,110 in the aggregate for the employee's own quarantine or symptoms, and $200 per day and $2,000 in the aggregate for caring for others. The Emergency Family and Medical Leave Expansion Act provides up to 12 weeks to care for a child under 18 whose school or child care is closed, for employees with at least 30 calendar days of service, the first 10 days unpaid and later days at not less than two-thirds of pay, capped at $200 per day and $10,000 in the aggregate. Legal references are PL 116-127 § 5101 et seq. and § 3101 et seq., 134 Stat. 177, and Executive Orders 2020-35 and 2020-36. The policy expires December 31, 2020 unless state or federal law extends the date.

## Item 5.F - Oakland Intermediate School District 2020-2021 budget

Section 624 of the Revised School Code requires the ISD to submit its proposed budget by May 1 and each constituent board to adopt a resolution of support or disapproval by June 1. Troy expresses support while stating that its support is for the sole purpose of complying with Section 624 and that the Intermediate School District is responsible for its own operations, including adoption of its budget. The transmittal letter of March 24, 2020 from Superintendent Dr. Wanda Cook-Robinson projects growth in Oakland Schools property tax revenues of 3.25%, tempered by a possible Headlee rollback of the operating millage measured against the Consumer Price Index. Literacy Essentials Oakland, prompted by declining 3rd grade M-STEP reading levels, is a four-year, $5 million pre-K through 3rd grade initiative with all 28 constituent districts. The CTE allocation to LEAs was increased by more than 25% in 2019-20 and continues in 2020-21. Shared services cover technology for thirteen (13) districts and business office services for five (5); Illuminate Education has served all twenty-eight (28) districts and two (2) public school academies since Fall of 2016 with a 50% subsidy again in 2020-21. Personnel costs carry step increases plus a 1.0% across-the-board increase; the Basic/MIP with Health Care Premium Subsidy retirement rate rises from 27.5% to 28.21% on October 1, 2020, with a blended rate projected at 28.0%. Health care hard caps are $18,596.96 family, $14,260.37 individual plus one and $6,818.87 single after 1/1/20, projected at $19,154.87, $14,688.18 and $7,023.44 after 1/1/21 assuming medical price index growth of 3.0%. PA-18 base special education distribution is budgeted to increase approximately $10.0 million, or 7.9%, with $3.5 million more for group homes, startup, extraordinary expenditures and capital, following $3.39 million above base in FY 2019-20.

Under Public Act 419 of 2004 and MCL 380.614, intermediate board members are elected biennially on the first Monday in June by an electoral body of one designee per constituent district, on a resolution adopted not earlier than 21 days before the election. Troy supports Mr. George Ehlert for the one (1) position, a term of six (6) years ending June 30, 2026, directing its representative to vote for him at least on the first ballot. Filing closed May 1, 2020 and resolutions were due May 29, 2020; balloting is in person 5:30-7:30 PM June 1, 2020 at the Oakland Schools Conference Center, 2111 Pontiac Lake Road, Waterford, with no absentee ballots and oath of office July 7, 2020. **Item 8.A — Resolution to submit replacement operating millage proposal.** The Board determined it necessary for continuing operation to restore and replace the authority to levy 18 mills for operating purposes on non-homestead property, previously approved by voters in 2015 and rolled back by application of the Headlee Amendment to the Michigan Constitution, and to increase the prior authority in the event of future rollbacks. The proposal is to be submitted at the General School Election of November 6, 2018, and the ballot wording must be certified to the Clerk of the County of Oakland, State of Michigan — the School District Election Coordinator — not later than August 14, 2018, as required by Act 116, Public Acts of Michigan, 1954, as amended. The resolution directs the Election Coordinator to post and publish notice of the last day of registration and notice of election and to have ballots prepared and printed in the form of Exhibit A, and rescinds conflicting resolutions. It is signed by Gary Hauff, Secretary, Board of Education, with a certification that the resolution was adopted at a regular meeting held July 17, 2018 in compliance with the Open Meetings Act, Act 267, Public Acts of Michigan, 1976. Exhibit A, the Replacement Operating Millage Proposal for the Troy School District, County of Oakland, State of Michigan, explains that the proposal would restore and replace the authority to levy the statutory limit of 18 mills on non-homestead property (principally industrial and commercial real property and residential rental property), which currently expires with the district's 2025 tax levy, and allow continued levy of the statutory limit of 18 mills in the event of future Headlee rollbacks of up to 3 mills, allowing the district to continue receiving revenues at the full per pupil foundation allowance permitted by the State. Owner occupied homes and qualified agricultural property are exempt. The ballot question asks whether the limitation on total taxes assessed against all property except principal residences and other property exempted by law within the Troy School District be increased in the amount of 21 mills, with 18 mills being the maximum allowable levy ($18.00 on each $1,000 of taxable valuation), for a period of eight (8) years, 2018 to 2025 inclusive, with 17.684 mills of the 21 mills being a replacement of authorized millage that would otherwise expire on December 31, 2025 and 0.316 mills being a restoration of millage lost as a result of the reduction required by the Michigan Constitution. The proposal states that the operating millage, if approved and levied, would provide estimated revenues to the School District of $22,644,260 during the 2018 calendar year, to be used for general operating purposes.

FICA remains 7.65%; PA 152 health caps for 2020 equal 2019 limits increased 1.0%. Purchased services rise 2.3% (about $469,000) and supplies 5.9% (about $426,000). **General Fund figures.** Audited 6/30/2018: revenue $151,774,253, expenditures $150,737,172, $1,037,081 surplus, ending fund equity $25,242,472 (16.75%). Final 6/30/2019 amendment: revenue $154,394,746, expenditures $155,576,715, ($1,181,969), ending equity $24,060,503 (15.47%). Recommended 6/30/2020: revenue $157,288,640, expenditures $158,261,349, ($972,709), ending equity $23,087,794 (14.59%). Revenue by source for 2019-20: local $40,561,662, state $103,282,321, federal $4,216,617, incoming transfers and other $9,228,040. Expenditures by object: salaries $77,189,826, benefits $50,286,826, purchased services $20,620,857, supplies $7,751,605, capital outlay $333,269, other $224,816, outgoing transfers $1,854,150. By function: basic programs $84,075,673 (elementary $35,163,550, middle school $19,518,132, high school $28,878,426), added needs $21,980,397 (special education $14,526,781, compensatory $6,673,785, career and technical $779,831), adult/continuing education $790,292, total instruction $106,846,362; support services $51,191,443, including pupil $10,924,985, instructional staff $9,124,866, school administration $8,499,351, operations and maintenance $10,776,242, pupil transportation $3,861,809 and central services $3,173,290; community services $223,544. The ten-year history runs from 2010-11 revenue of $137,351,597 and expenditures of $137,073,867 to projected 2019-20 revenue of $156,086,440, with the fund balance percentage moving from 14.4% in 2010-11 to a projected 14.6%.

**Other funds, 2019-20.** Food Service: revenues $3,455,890 (local $2,281,500, state $107,000, federal $1,067,390), expenditures $3,435,345, transfers out $20,000, ending balance $4,690. Troy Career Center: state $60,000, federal $2,385,150, expenditures $2,400,150 plus $45,000 transfers out, zero balance. Adult Education and Community Service: local $3,021,900, expenditures $1,952,976, transfers out $1,100,000, ending balance $544,954; by program, Continuing Education $630,000 and CARE Co. $2,391,900 in revenue. Facility Rentals: local $135,000, expenditures $161,780, ending balance $246,925. Troy School District Preschool: local $2,021,500, expenditures $1,996,615 including $233,615 debt service, ending balance $69,180. Troy School and Student Activities: $5,000,000 in and out, ending balance $2,000,000. Debt Service Funds: property taxes $16,210,086, investment earnings $45,000, state $192,514, total $16,447,600; principal $12,235,000, interest $5,503,110, other bond expenditures $2,500, total $17,740,610, ending balance $1,124,544. By fund, expenditures are $4,708,156 (2012 Fund 312), $3,878,000 (2014 Fund 314), $4,408,250 (2015 Fund 315), $2,672,140 (2016 Fund 316) and $2,074,064 (2019 Fund 319). The debt payment schedule through 2039-40 totals $146,700,000 principal and $42,178,225.89 interest, $188,878,225.89 combined. Capital funds: 2016 Capital Projects (Series II) capital outlay $8,832,462; Early Childhood Learning Center building and site improvements $6,068,633 plus furniture and equipment $1,071,300 with $5,232,000 sale of land; 2019 Capital Projects (Series III) capital outlay $5,000,000 leaving $22,168,593 after $26,998,655 of bond proceeds; Capital Maintenance purchased services $500,000 leaving $496,469; Sinking Fund revenue $4,030,000 and capital outlay $3,828,500, leaving $201,500. Grants described include At-Risk, Bilingual Education, CFE Millage, Early Literacy, Great Start Readiness, IDEA-Flowthrough, IDEA-Preschool, Titles I through IV and Workforce Investment Act funds tied to Oakland County Michigan Works!

**2018-19 budget amendment.** Amended appropriations: General Fund $155,576,715; Food Service $4,334,204; Adult Education and Community Service $3,816,201; Preschool $381,705; Facilities Rental $748,176; Capital Maintenance $190,000; 2014 Capital Projects $107,185; 2016 Capital Projects $15,320,000; 2019 Capital Projects $130,062; Early Childhood Learning Center Capital Projects $13,000,000; Sinking Fund $3,882,000; Debt Service $15,399,958. General Fund revenue moves from $153,199,134 to $154,394,746, a change of $1,195,612, and expenditures from $155,009,522 to $155,576,715, a change of $567,193, lifting projected June 30 fund balance from $23,432,084 to $24,060,503. State revenue rose $926,625; pupil support rose $293,757; pupil transportation fell $140,128; the Early Childhood Learning Center sale-of-land estimate dropped $3,283,000 to $372,413.

**2019-20 appropriations resolution.** General Fund $158,261,349; Food Service $3,455,345; Troy Career Center $2,445,150; Adult Education and Community Service $3,052,976; Preschool $1,996,615; Facilities Rental $161,780; Troy School and Student Activities $5,000,000; Capital Maintenance $500,000; 2016 Capital Projects $8,582,462; 2019 Capital Projects $5,000,000; Early Childhood Learning Center Capital Projects $5,232,000; Sinking Fund $3,828,500; Debt Service $17,740,610. Certified millage: non-homestead 18.0000, commercial personal property 10.8836, homestead 4.8836, debt retirement 4.1000, sinking fund 0.9857.

**Consent and curriculum.** The December 18, 2018 Bid Pack #23 resolution is amended so the $5,818,684.50 award is an expenditure of the 2016 Capital Projects Fund, Sinking Fund and Food Service Fund. Awards covered Schroeder, Troy Union, Smith, International Academy East and Troy High and included BNE Masonry $349,100.00, Men of Steel $48,000.00, Advanced Building Group $394,319.00, JD Candler Roofing $20,310.00, Hewett Company $434,249.00, Continental Contracting $209,500.00, Seven Brothers Painting $49,584.00, Great Lakes Hotel Supply $266,495.00, CMS Mechanical $881,133.00, Contrast Mechanical $990,000.00, MCMI $598,050.00, Great Lakes Power & Lighting $767,000.00, Brencal Contracting $306,200.00 and contingency of $504,744.50, reviewed by TSD Operations, TMP Associates, Peter Basso & Associates and Barton Malow. Jennifer Gottlieb, Director of Student Growth, Equity and Accountability, presented the grades 6-8 science adoption of SEPUP Science Kits at $507,182.50 following a June 4 special board workshop; piloted programs were SEPUP (Lab-Aids), IQWST (Activate Learning), HMH Science Dimensions, FOSS (Delta Education) and Cereal City Science, reviewed with a modified EQUIP rubric published by Achieve and aligned to NGSS on the district's seven-year adoption cycle.

**Business awards.** Niles Center roof replacement (Public Bid 9889) goes to Royal West Roofing at a base bid of $163,000.00, total request $179,300.00 including 10% contingency from the 2016 Capital Projects Fund; Rob Carson, Director of Maintenance and Operations, and WeatherTech Consulting Group (Peter Kinnunen) recommended it after a 5/14/19 pre-bid conference and two sealed bids opened 5/23/19, the other from Schena Roofing. Telecommunications go to TelNet Worldwide for 2019/2020, 2020/2021 and 2021/2022, replacing PRI circuits with SIP trunking; Beth Soggs, Director of Technology, and consultants Abilita evaluated eight bids received 5/23/2019, citing TelNet's estimated monthly recurring cost of approximately $1,076.50 before surcharges, burstable capacity from 36 to 50 talk paths, Troy headquarters and compatibility with the Mitel Connect system. Secondary computer lab upgrades total $103,619.00 from the 2016 Capital Projects Fund: $86,802.00 in monitors from Presidio via the MHEC contract and $16,817.00 in SSDs and RAM from Logical Ram Solutions, covering 721 22-inch monitors, 52 27-inch monitors and 335 SSD and RAM upgrades at Baker, Boulan, Larson, Smith, Athens, Troy High and TCCHS. The district will buy 1,250 iPads from Apple at $294 each for $367,500 via the REMC SPOT bid and 1,056 Rug-Ed cases at $22 each for $23,232, funded from the 2016 Capital Projects Fund and the Preschool Fund. Preschool laptops and desktops from Presidio total $39,823.00, including 26 Dell Latitude 3300 laptops at $621.00 each. First Student's transportation contract is extended three years from July 1, 2019 to June 30, 2022 with zero rate increases in 2019-2020 and 2020-2021 and 1.25% in 2021-2022, a $5,000 new-bus credit spread $2,000/$2,000/$1,000, and renegotiation if the 5-tier system converts to 3 or 4 tiers; the April 1, 2019 letter is from Area General Manager Douglas Meek. A tractor/loader goes to Rochester Lawn Equipment for $30,969.12 under MiDEAL contract 071B7700085.

**Personnel and closing.** Natalie Haezebrouck is recommended for a two-year probationary administrative contract without tenure as Director of Teaching and Learning effective July 1, 2019. She began in Troy in 2005 as a 2nd grade teacher at Leonard and Schroeder Elementary Schools, became a Literacy Specialist at Leonard, and is a Curriculum and Instruction Specialist; she received the State of Michigan Elementary Literacy Teacher of the Year award in 2016 and holds degrees from Western Michigan University, Oakland University and Madonna University. Six applicants were interviewed (Joyce Brasington, Sarah Fairman, Megan Foster, Natalie Haezebrouck, Jeremy Whan, Stephanie Zendler) and three advanced. The meeting closed with Superintendent Dr. Rich Machesky introducing the "2018-2019 School Year in Review" video.

RECOGNITION. Mr. Leonard Rezmierski, Michigan American Red Cross Board Member, and Mrs. Kelly DeLong, Michigan American Red Cross Donor Recruitment Representative, presented a "Certificate of Recognition" for the district's support of Michigan Red Cross programs; Troy High senior Ian Watson was credited with assisting. Spring 2019 all-state athletes recognized by Mr. Fulcher: Jenna Doyle (Senior, Athens HS Track & Field, coach Tom Cook), Lauren Fulcher (Senior, Troy HS Track & Field, Matt Richardson), Cameron Graziosi (Junior, Athens HS Track & Field, Mike Stallsmith), Grace Johnson (Junior, Troy HS Track & Field, Matt Richardson), Alexis Morse and Sahaja Pinnu (Seniors, Troy HS Girls Tennis, Brian Miska), Jordyn Rauser and Brooke Russell (Seniors, Athens HS Girls Soccer, Todd Heugh), Agata Szewczuk (Senior, Athens HS Girls Tennis, Jennifer Yetter), Tahra Brodbine (Senior, Troy HS Girls Soccer, Dan Troccoli) and Morgan MacDonald (Senior, Troy HS Girls Lacrosse, Holly Frederick). The Association of School Business Officials International awarded its Certificate of Excellence in Financial Reporting for the Comprehensive Annual Financial Report for the fiscal year ended June 30, 2018; the certificate is signed by ASBO President Tom Wohlleber, CSRM, and Executive Director David J. Lewis, whose September 12, 2019 letter to Rick West, Assistant Superintendent, Business Services, notes review-team comments that must be answered in next year's application packet. President Schmidt called the workshop to order at 5:12 p.m. with Fleming, Gottlieb, Hauff, Philippart and Wilson present, Hammond absent, Superintendent Machesky and administrators West, Harris, DiPilato, Birmingham, Griffor and Carrier attending, and three audience members; topics were compensation packages and Niles program relocation; adjourned 6:04 p.m. The regular meeting opened at 6:13 p.m. with four audience members. Resolution 19-074 (Hauff/Fleming) approved the July 16, 2019 minutes, the May/June 2019 Treasurer's Report, IA-East Schools of Choice Section 105C for 9th grade for 2020/2021, and the Oakland County School Boards Association legislative priorities; Yes 6, No 0, Hammond absent. Resolution 19-075 (Philippart/Hauff) extended the Superintendent's contract from July 1, 2019 through June 30, 2024 without tenure. Resolution 19-076 (Wilson/Fleming) extended contracts for Rick West (Business Services), Kris Griffor (Elementary Instruction) and Jordan Harris (Employee Services) through June 2021. Bloomfield Hills Public Schools officials Howard Baron (Treasurer), Jennifer Cook (Trustee) and Lisa Efros (Secretary) addressed International Academy governance, the complaint against the International Academy Joint Steering Committee, and the IA Task Force. Resolution 19-077 (Fleming/Philippart) moved the January 14, 2020 meeting to January 21, 2020. Resolution 19-078 (Philippart/Hauff) authorized closed session under the Open Meetings Act, Public Act 267, Section 8(c) for attorney-client privilege; roll call yes from Fleming, Gottlieb, Hauff, Philippart, Schmidt and Wilson, Hammond absent. He identifies humility, integrity and vision as the three most important personal characteristics. He writes that educational leadership requires humility and a keen focus on service toward improving outcomes for learners, that selflessness and appreciation for collaboration are essential, and that servant leadership causes educators and stakeholders to sense their value and contribute toward common goals, whereas ego-driven leadership breeds competitive and hostile environments in which individuals fight for their own agendas rather than a shared vision. Question 2 asks how important technology is in education and what technology-related skills the applicant can contribute. He argues technology must remain a supplement to human understanding and connection rather than a replacement, comparing the Information Age to the eras revolutionized by the pencil and the printing press, and notes that the available wealth of knowledge includes voices previously stifled by oppressive and marginalizing forces. He concludes that when technology supplements critical thinking, learners add depth to breadth and learn to hold varying ideas in tension while remaining grounded in empirical truths.

Meeting and Attendance
Troy Board of Education meeting, Troy, Michigan, November 17, 2020, held remotely via Zoom Webinar with public notice posted to allow remote community participation. President Schmidt called the meeting to order at 7:00 p.m. Present via Zoom in addition to Mr. Schmidt were Board members Anne, Gottlieb, Hammond, Hauff, Philippart and Wilson. Also present were Superintendent Machesky; administrators Birmingham, Carrier, Griffor, DiPilato, Roncone, Haezebrouck, House, Pagel and West; two Student Board Reps; and approximately 48 additional members of the audience.

Recognition
TSD Mission Moment honoring Troy High School English teachers Jodie Duda, Erin Fischer-Ballew, Annie Gallagher, Christina Rick and Valerie Valentino, recipients of a Michigan Council of Teachers of English (MCTE) Diversity, Inclusion, Justice and Equity (DIJE) professional development grant. Their reading program includes Black Appetite. White Food by Jamila Lyiscott; We Got This. by Cornelius Miner; The Anti-Racist Teacher: Reading Instruction Workbook by Lorena German; Educating Activist Allies by Katy Swalwell; and Linguistic Justice by April Baker-Bell.

Public Communication
There were no additions or deletions. Andrew Rodman, Troy resident and parent of two Martell Elementary School students, addressed the Board about the decision to move elementary students back to remote learning and when they plan to return to in-seat. No one spoke during non-agenda public communication.

Actions
| No. | Item | Mover / Support | Vote |
|---|---|---|---|
| 20-084 | Consent agenda items A, B, C | Hauff / Hammond | 7-0 |
| 20-085 | Building signage award, Johnson Sign Company, $92,000 | Anne / Philippart | 7-0 |
| 20-086 | Bus purchase, Hoekstra Transportation, $1,687,276.00 | Philippart / Anne | 7-0 |
| 20-087 | Reconfirmation of COVID-19 Preparedness and Response Plan | Wilson / Philippart | 6-1, Hammond No |
| 20-088 | Open Meetings Act resolution on Senate Bill 1108 | Philippart / Hauff | 7-0 |

The consent agenda covered minutes of the October 6, 2020 Board Workshop, minutes of the October 20, 2020 Board Meeting, and the Treasurer's Report for September 2020. The signage award covers refurbishment of the school messaging sign at Athens High School and new messaging signs at the Troy Preschool and Troy Learning Center, inclusive of 6% contingency, charged to the 2019 Capital Projects Fund and/or the Sinking Fund. The bus award is charged to the 2019 Capital Projects Fund; discussion covered bus end-of-life cycle and resale value, and grants for electric buses, which Mr. West explained would be cost-prohibitive at this time.

Other Business
Dr. Machesky presented an update on the District's extended learning plan with PowerPoint slides on climbing COVID case counts in Michigan and Oakland County, with additional updates from Ms. Birmingham, Mrs. Griffor and Mrs. DiPilato. https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
Minutes of the Board of Education, Troy, Michigan, Board Meeting of November 17, 2020, held via Zoom Webinar. The meeting was held remotely and a public notice was posted in order to allow community members to participate remotely. President Schmidt called the meeting to order at 7:00 p.m. In addition to Mr. Schmidt, present via Zoom videoconference were Board members Anne, Gottlieb, Hammond, Hauff, Philippart and Wilson. Also present were Superintendent Machesky; administrators Birmingham, Carrier, Griffor, DiPilato, Roncone, Haezebrouck, House, Pagel and West; two Student Board Reps; and approximately 48 additional members of the audience.

RECOGNITION - TSD MISSION MOMENT
The Michigan Council of Teachers of English (MCTE) Diversity, Inclusion, Justice, and Equity (DIJE) subcommittee awarded Jodie Duda, Erin Fischer-Ballew, Annie Gallagher, Christina Rick, and Valerie Valentino of Troy High School a DIJE professional development grant. The stated goal of the grant is to support Michigan English teachers across the state as they engage in professional development they design that privileges diversity, inclusion, justice, and equity work. The recipients created a program of reading and learning supporting their commitment to disrupting stock stories, stereotypes, and westernized narratives. Their selected texts are Black Appetite. White Food: Issues of Race, Voice and Justice Within and Beyond the Classroom, by Jamila Lyiscott; We Got This.: Equity, Access, and the Quest to Be Who Our Students Need Us to Be, by Cornelius Miner; The Anti-Racist Teacher: Reading Instruction Workbook, by Lorena German; Educating Activist Allies: Social Justice Pedagogy with the Suburban and Urban Elite, by Katy Swalwell; and Linguistic Justice: Black Language, Literacy, Identity, and Pedagogy, by April Baker-Bell. Their intention is to use the concepts and practice presented in their readings to plan learning for their students to build community and engage in rich activist lives.

ADDITIONS AND DELETIONS
None.

PUBLIC COMMUNICATION
Andrew Rodman, Troy resident and parent of two students who attend Martell Elementary School, addressed the Board about the decision to move elementary students back to remote learning and when they plan to return to in-seat.

GENERAL - CONSENT AGENDA (Resolution 20-084)
It was moved by Mr. Hauff and supported by Mrs. Hammond that the Troy Board of Education approve items A, B, and C on the consent agenda: minutes of the October 6, 2020 Board of Education Workshop; minutes of the October 20, 2020 Board of Education Meeting; and the Treasurer's Report for September 2020. On roll call vote, Schmidt Yes, Wilson Yes, Anne Yes, Gottlieb Yes, Hammond Yes, Hauff Yes, Philippart Yes. Yes: 7, No: 0.

PERSONNEL AND CURRICULUM
No items were recorded under Personnel or Curriculum.

BUSINESS - BUILDING SIGNAGE (Resolution 20-085)
It was moved by Mrs. Anne and supported by Dr. Philippart that the bid for signage for the refurbishment of the school messaging sign at Athens High School and new messaging signs at the Troy Preschool and Troy Learning Center be awarded to Johnson Sign Company in the amount of $92,000 (inclusive of 6% contingency), and that this amount be approved as an expenditure of the 2019 Capital Projects Fund and/or the Sinking Fund. On roll call vote, Wilson Yes, Anne Yes, Gottlieb Yes, Hammond Yes, Hauff Yes, Philippart Yes, Schmidt Yes. Yes: 7, No: 0.

BUSINESS - BUS PURCHASE (Resolution 20-086)
It was moved by Dr. Philippart and supported by Mrs. Anne that the bid for school buses be awarded to Hoekstra Transportation in the amount of $1,687,276.00 and that this amount be approved as an expenditure of the 2019 Capital Projects Fund. There was discussion about the end of life cycle for buses and how much money the District could sell them for. There was also discussion about looking into grants for electric buses; however, Mr. West explained that it would be cost-prohibitive at this time. On roll call vote, Anne Yes, Gottlieb Yes, Hammond Yes, Hauff Yes, Philippart Yes, Schmidt Yes, Wilson Yes. Yes: 7, No: 0.

PUBLIC COMMUNICATION - NON-AGENDA ITEMS
None.

OTHER - EXTENDED LEARNING PLAN
Dr. Machesky shared an update on the District's extended learning plan and provided PowerPoint slides showing the most recent numbers in COVID cases and how much they had been climbing in Michigan and in Oakland County. Ms. Birmingham, Mrs. Griffor and Mrs. DiPilato also shared updates from their respective areas, and there was further discussion among Board members.

RECONFIRMATION OF COVID-19 PREPAREDNESS AND RESPONSE PLAN (Resolution 20-087)
The minutes recite that Governor Whitmer's Executive Order 2020-142 provides a structure to support all schools in Michigan as they plan for a return of Pre-K through Post High School education in the fall, and that under this order Michigan school districts must adopt a COVID-19 Preparedness and Response Plan laying out how they will cope with the disease across the various phases of the Michigan Safe Start Plan. Each district must submit a reconfirmation plan to its Board of Education for approval on a monthly basis, and once approved must post its Preparedness Plan on the district website home page for public access. It was moved by Dr. Wilson and supported by Dr. Philippart that the Troy Board of Education approve the District's Reconfirmation of the COVID-19 Preparedness and Response Plan. On roll call vote, Gottlieb Yes, Hammond No, Hauff Yes, Philippart Yes, Schmidt Yes, Wilson Yes, Anne Yes. Yes: 6, No: 1.

OPEN MEETINGS ACT RESOLUTION (Resolution 20-088)
It was moved by Dr. Philippart and supported by Mr. Hauff. The whereas clauses state that Michigan Senate Bill 1108 of 2020 amended the State's Open Meetings Act to restrict the reasons a member of a public body may attend a public meeting remotely beginning January 1, 2021; that advancing technology enabled school districts across the State to meet remotely during the COVID-19 pandemic, to develop and implement plans to educate students safely and effectively, and to ensure safe and effective public participation; that the restrictions in Senate Bill 1108 allow remote attendance after December 31, 2021 only for absence due to military duty; that threats to public health and other disasters will not vanish on December 31, 2020, and that contagious diseases, flooding, tornadoes, acts of terrorism or other causes occurring after that date could make it unsafe or impossible for public bodies to meet in person or for some members to attend in person; that not allowing an immune-compromised member of a public body to participate remotely would be a clear violation of the Reasonable Accommodation clause of the Federal Americans with Disabilities Act; and that decisions about situations that may or may not merit remote attendance by members of a local public body are best determined by that body and the community it represents rather than the State Legislature.

The resolved clauses urge the Legislature to ideally amend Senate Bill 1108, Sec. 3a(b) to include a provision requiring local public bodies to set their own policies regarding remote meeting participation based on the needs and priorities of their own local communities rather than dictating universal policy to all public bodies in the State without regard to local control; urge the Legislature at a minimum to amend Senate Bill 1108, Sec. 3a(b) to extend indefinitely its provisions allowing remote attendance to accommodate absence due to a medical condition or a statewide or local state of emergency or state of disaster, in addition to military service, and to add accommodations for family emergencies and work obligations; and direct the Board Secretary to transmit copies of the resolution within five business days of adoption to Senator Mallory McMorrow, Representative Padma Kuppa, Oakland Schools Intermediate School District, and the Michigan Association of School Boards. On roll call vote, Hammond Yes, Hauff Yes, Philippart Yes, Schmidt Yes, Wilson Yes, Anne Yes, Gottlieb Yes. Yes: 7, No: 0.

BOARD COMMENTS
Mrs. Hammond spoke about the events that happened during the last Board meeting, said how unfair it was presented, and stated that she will continue to advocate for what she believes in. Dr. Wilson thanked the teachers and administrators for their hard work in making things go as smoothly as possible. Dr. Philippart announced that the TFEE is holding a pandemic-safe fundraiser offering a raffle for $1,000 worth of gift cards, with tickets available for $5 each. Mr. Gottlieb thanked the TSD staff and fellow board members for all they are doing during these trying times. Mr. Hauff thanked veterans for their sacrifice and service, thanked the Central Office staff and hardworking teachers, and said oneTROY is the greatest school district in Michigan. Mrs. Anne thanked everyone for all they are doing during these difficult times.

REPORTS FROM STUDENT REPRESENTATIVES
Pranay Gupta, student representative from International Academy - East, reported on what is happening with students learning virtually in his school. Nathania Nartey, student representative from Athens High School, reported on what is happening with students now that they are 100% virtual. Sejal Patel, student representative from Troy High School, was not in attendance. Carleton Thomas, student representative from Troy College and Career High School, was not in attendance.

ADJOURNMENT
Dr. Machesky thanked the Board for their continued efforts to support the District's work and for their help in supporting the LIVE program. He congratulated Bemis Elementary School for being recognized as a National Blue Ribbon School for the second time and wished everyone a Happy Thanksgiving. Mr. Schmidt wished everyone a Happy Thanksgiving and announced that the next Board Workshop would be held on December 1st at 6:00 p.m. via Zoom. The meeting was adjourned at 8:45 p.m. The minutes were respectfully submitted by Gary N. Hauff, Secretary, Troy Board of Education, with the preparation notation GH/jh.

Solicitation. The memorandum states the district issued Request for Proposals (RFP) #9881 for Custodial, Grounds & Warehouse Services on March 21, 2019. Proposals were due April 4, 2019, and five (5) competitive proposals were received. Rob Carson, Larry Franckowiak and Rick West reviewed and analyzed the submitted proposals and selected ABM, D.M. Burr and GDI to interview.

Interviews. On April 18, 2019 a committee conducted interviews of the three selected companies. The committee consisted of Nicole Wilson, Bob Dowd, Joe Duda, Sarah Glasser, Larry Franckowiak, Rob Carson, Jim Crowley and Rick West. Each company was provided approximately a one-hour interview in which it presented its proposal and engaged in a Q&A session with the committee. The memorandum notes each committee member brought a unique perspective and provided valuable input to assist in making a recommendation.

Evaluation outcome. Although the committee was not a decision-making body, a general level of discomfort was conveyed with the proposal and presentation submitted by GDI. The committee felt that both ABM and D.M. Burr were qualified to service the District. The committee discussed the cost associated with both proposals and each member's experience with transitioning service providers, and recommended that Rob Carson and Rick West further review the costs of each proposal and explore the possibility of negotiating a successor agreement with DM Burr.

Overtime treatment. In further reviewing the costs associated with the ABM and DM Burr proposals, the district asked both companies to provide the number of assumed overtime hours in their proposals needed to adequately cover all events requested by the District, and a new proposed number if the District were to bill overtime as a direct pass through. Rob Carson and Rick West state their belief that it is in the district's best interest to have the successful contractor begin to bill overtime hours as a direct pass through as opposed to including overtime in the contract price.

Wage structure. The RFP asked each company to cost out its proposal at a $12, $13 and $14 beginning wage for custodians. The memorandum notes that each of the companies stated that the current labor market in Troy would require a $13 minimum wage to recruit and retain custodians.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.paragraph: Slide presentation delivered to the Troy Board of Education on August 5, 2020, reporting the work of the district Return to Learn task forces organized around the MI Return to School Road Map. Four workgroups covering safety protocols, operations, instruction, and mental health and social-emotional well-being present recommendations for the 2020-21 school year, including universal masking, cleaning and screening protocols, and a redesigned secondary 3x3 block schedule. The core instructional design is a single daily schedule that works identically across Michigan Safe Start Phases 1 through 6, supported by 1:1 iPads for all students in grades K-12 and delivery through Schoology and Zoom. A special Board meeting on Wednesday, August 12 was scheduled to approve the plan.

**Meeting and framing**
Presented at the Troy School District Board of Education meeting of August 5, 2020, under the banner Return to Learn and anchored to the MI Return to School Road Map, described as built by public health experts and flexible to changing conditions.

**Goals and guiding principles**
Goals: students return to face-to-face instruction as soon as possible; safety and sustainability; consistent programming. Guiding principles: Troy teachers lead learning; build classroom communities; attend to social/emotional needs; maximum flexibility for families; collaborative effort.

**Task force structure**

| Strand | Leads |
| --- | --- |
| Safety Protocols | Rick West and Jordan Harris |
| Operations | Rick West and Jordan Harris |
| Instruction | Kris Griffor and Christine DiPilato |
| Mental Health and Social Emotional Well-Being | Jessica Carrier |

**Safety and operations**
Masks required for all school staff, visitors, and all students on buses, inside buildings, and anywhere on school grounds when individuals may be within 6 feet; all students K-Post High required to wear masks all day. Exceptions cover incapacitation, inability to remove a mask unaided, an approved medical or behavioral health exemption with a physician note, eating or drinking, and outdoor strenuous physical activity with social distancing. Supplies cited: 5,000 adult disposable masks on hand with 50,000 on order, 52,000 kid-size disposable masks on order, and 4,300 face shields on hand. Hand-washing for at least 20 seconds is encouraged; frequently touched surfaces sanitized between classes, at least every 4 hours, and at day's end. More than $10 million has been invested in HVAC systems in the past 7 years. Elementary classroom workspaces shown 6 feet apart; a high school classroom 3 feet apart. Student lockers prohibited in grades 6-12; three Registered Nurses available for COVID-19 response. Staff and students stay home with a fever of 100.4 degrees or more; guidance follows the Oakland County Health Division, MDHHS, and CDC.

**Instructional plan**
Three scenarios align to state phases: Virtual Learning (Phases 1-3, schools closed to student attendance, 100% virtual); Transition to Return Plan (Phases 4/5, 50% of students in-seat and 50% virtual, cohorted by last name, buildings open 4 days with all students virtual Wednesdays); and In-Seat Learning Plan (Phases 4/5/6, 100% of students in-seat, buildings open 5 days). All three use 3 periods per day and 90-minute class periods with live instruction via Zoom. Return to regularly scheduled programming is listed as September 2021.

**Technology**
The Board voted to move forward with 1:1 iPads for all students in grades K-12, with a keyboard, and an iPad kit for every teacher including interactive stylus, keyboard, and stand for live capture. Schoology is the learning management system K-12; Zoom is the virtual delivery platform. There will be no separate stand-alone virtual program.

**Schedules**
Secondary moves to an A Day (hours 1-3) / B Day (hours 4-6) rotation with 90-minute blocks, 20-minute advisory, and 60-minute student support or teacher collaboration blocks; classes meet 5 times over a two-week rotation. First class starts at regular times: HS 7:20, Early MS 7:54, Late MS 8:19. During 50% attendance, last names A-K attend in person Monday and Tuesday and L-Z attend Thursday and Friday, with all students virtual Wednesday.

**Start of year and next steps**
Tuesday 9/1 is the first day for K, 6, and 9 only; 9/2 and 9/3 are half days by cohort; 9/4 no school; 9/7 Labor Day; 9/8 first full day. Next steps: staff Q&A Thursday, presentation to parents Thursday, a Return to Learn Community Conversation Monday, August 10 live on Facebook, and a special Board meeting Wednesday, August 12 to approve the plan.

MENTAL HEALTH AND SEL. Supports for students and families include a student self-report mental health survey, the district screener SRSS administered three times a year, daily check-ins, the ONETroy Community Resources Document, staff and family resources, and TSD Cares on-line resources. Staff supports include a staff self-awareness survey, wellness resources, district and building support systems, the Employee Assistance Program, staff development in trauma, socio-emotional learning and equity and inclusion, and protocols for responding to student concerns or crisis at the building level.

PERSONAL PROTECTIVE EQUIPMENT. Masks must be worn by all school staff, visitors, and all students on buses or other transportation, inside school buildings, and anywhere on school grounds including outside when individuals may be within 6 feet of each other. All students K-Post High are required to wear masks all day, in classrooms as well as common areas. Exceptions are someone incapacitated or unconscious, someone unable to remove a mask without assistance, someone approved for a medical or behavioral health exemption with a physician note, anyone eating or drinking, and students in outdoor strenuous physical activity while practicing social distancing. Masks are subject to the Troy School District dress code. Disposable masks will be available on buses and in buildings: 5,000 adult disposable masks on hand with 50,000 on order, and 52,000 kid-size disposable masks on order. Disposable gloves will be available in buildings; 4,300 face shields are on hand; safety barriers are being explored for specific spaces and protective wear such as gowns for specific classrooms.

CLEANING AND HYGIENE. Students are encouraged to wash hands for at least 20 seconds often, after using the bathroom and before eating or drinking. Frequently touched surfaces will be sanitized between classes, at least every 4 hours, and at the end of the day; student desks cleaned between use. Sanitizer stations will be available throughout each building and checklists used to confirm stations and soap dispensers are filled and sinks working. On HVAC systems, the district reports investing more than $10 million in the past 7 years into reliable and safe systems at all school buildings, with routine filter changes.

SPACING, MOVEMENT AND ACCESS. Classroom seating will be separated as much as possible and/or face the same direction; elementary workspaces shown are 6 feet apart and a high school classroom is shown at 3 feet apart. Visitors are limited to essential functions, must call the office for entry, and are screened with a temperature check and questionnaire. Assemblies, field trips, and similar large-group activities are temporarily prohibited. Floor and wall markings, signage, and one-way hallway traffic are planned. Students are encouraged to bring their own water bottles. The district will have access to three (3) Registered Nurses to assist with COVID-19 response. Soft furnishings that cannot easily be disinfected will be removed from classrooms, and use of student lockers is prohibited in grades 6-12.

SCREENING AND POSITIVE CASES. Staff self-screen daily; a parent or guardian is expected to screen students daily. Staff and students should stay home if ill or with a fever of 100.4 degrees or more. Anyone who thinks or knows they have COVID-19 or had direct exposure should stay home and contact the building office, with next steps guided by the Oakland County Health Division, MDHHS, and CDC guidelines through the District Nurse Consultant. A student who becomes ill at school will be isolated in a designated area with a designated staff member until picked up by an authorized person. A person with an alternative diagnosis who is symptom-free and fever-free for 24 hours without fever-reducing medication may return. The Oakland County Health Department will notify schools of confirmed positive cases and close contacts will be notified as soon as possible; privacy of staff and students will be respected.

FOOD SERVICE, ATHLETICS, TRANSPORTATION. Indoor assemblies bringing together more than one classroom are prohibited; cafeterias and other large areas such as gymnasiums, media centers, and LGI rooms will be used for lunch, outdoor areas used where possible, menu items limited and most lunches prepackaged, meals available for virtual student pick-up, and lunch periods altered to reduce classes per period. Athletics will comply with all MHSAA guidance. Bus transportation is available within transportation boundaries; hand sanitizer is required before boarding with stations at each bus entrance, face coverings required, buses disinfected, and windows kept open weather permitting. Building-level administration has received a list of medically vulnerable students flagged in their building; virtual learning options are available to all families and medical plans on file may be updated.

SAFETY PROTOCOLS BY PHASE AND CHALLENGES. Phases 1-3 mean no in-person instruction. Phases 4, 5 and 6 carry face coverings for all staff and students, social distancing, no visitors in buildings, transportation with face coverings, modified lunch and recess, and strict cleaning and hygiene protocols. Major challenges listed are lack of guidance from the Oakland County Health Division on screening and response to positive tests, social distancing in classrooms, common areas and buses, cleaning of desks between use, lunch services, and budget uncertainties.

INSTRUCTIONAL SCENARIOS. Virtual Learning applies to Phases 1-3 with schools closed for student attendance, 3 periods per day, 90-minute class periods, live Zoom instruction for all courses, and 100% virtual attendance. The Transition to Return Plan applies to Phases 4/5 with 50% of students in-seat and 50% virtual, 3 periods per day, 90-minute classes, live instruction in person and via Zoom, cohorting by last name, buildings open 4 days for in-seat attendance, and all students virtual on Wednesdays. The In-Seat Learning Plan applies to Phases 4/5/6 with 100% of students in-seat, buildings open all 5 days. Return to regularly scheduled programming is listed as September 2021. Families may elect to keep students home to learn virtually all year or send them on the day aligned to student last name.

TECHNOLOGY. The Board voted to move forward with 1:1 iPads for all students in grades K-12; every student will have a dedicated device and keyboard, and every teacher an iPad kit including interactive stylus, keyboard and stand for live capture. Schoology is the K-12 learning management system and Zoom the virtual delivery platform. There will be no separate stand-alone virtual learning program.

SCHEDULES. Elementary components: literacy and math taught daily, science and social studies several times per week, access to all specials virtually, and built-in student support. Secondary components: A Day equals hours 1-3, B Day equals hours 4-6, 90-minute instructional blocks, student advisory, and student support. In the virtual secondary week, each day runs three 90-minute blocks with breaks, a 20-minute advisory, and either 60 minutes of student support or 60 minutes of teacher team collaboration and professional learning; first class starts in alignment with regular school start times of HS 7:20, Early MS 7:54, and Late MS 8:19. Classes meet 5 times over a two-week rotation. Stated benefits include one daily schedule that transitions across Phases 1-6, deeper 90-minute learning, adaptable passing time, a reduction in hall passing from 5 times to 2 times, HS starting at regular time and dismissing before lunch, and extended MS lunchtime for safety protocols; instructional considerations note comparable time in class versus a 6-period day, slightly less time per week but fewer transitions.

TRANSITION SCHEDULES. Under the Transition to Return Plan, teachers teach in the classroom daily with live capture via Zoom and interactive capability, attendance taken daily, last names A-K in seat Monday and Tuesday while L-Z attend virtually, last names L-Z in seat Thursday and Friday while A-K attend virtually, and all students virtual on Wednesday. The draft early middle school 50% in-seat schedule runs 1st or 4th hour (95 minutes) 7:55-9:30, 10-minute passing, 2nd or 5th hour (90) 9:40-11:10, 10-minute passing, 3rd or 6th hour (90) with lunch (25) 11:20-1:15, advisory (20) 1:25-1:45, buses at 1:45, and virtual student support or teacher collaboration 1:45-2:45; Wednesday runs 3rd hour (90) 11:20-12:50, teacher lunch 12:50-1:15, and student support and intervention 1:00-2:20. The draft high school 50% in-seat schedule runs 1st or 4th hour (95) 7:20-8:55, 2nd or 5th hour (95) 9:00-10:35, 3rd or 6th hour (95) 10:40-12:15, grab-to-go lunch with buses at 12:25, teacher duty-free lunch 12:20-12:45, advisory 12:50-1:10 (20 minutes) by appointment, and student support and intervention or teacher collaboration 1:10-2:20; Wednesday shifts to 2nd hour 9:05-10:40, 3rd hour 10:50-12:25, teacher lunch 12:30-1:00, and student support and intervention 1:00-2:20.

SPECIAL PROGRAMS. Troy College and Career High School aligns with the 3x3 block in an ABAB rotation, adds a morning session for student support and small group work, and moves first bell to a later 9:00 a.m. start, with additional information from Mr. Turner. International Academy East cites unique program needs, IB course requirements, three campuses, an A/B day rotation, in-seat determination by grade level (9/10 and 11/12), a virtual start on 8/20, and transition to in-seat courses on 8/31 in alignment with the TSD decision. For IFSP, IEP and 504 students from birth through post-high, the Roadmap highlights plans covering special education, birth-to-five services at the Early Childhood Center and Post-High at TCT, structures for general and special education teacher collaboration on assessments and instruction outlined in IEPs, assistive technologies, and continuation-of-service plans for social work, occupational, physical, and speech and language therapy including evaluations. Troy School District preschool programs will follow state and county guidance in accordance with licensing rules, prioritize students in seats for family supports, and offer virtual programming options.

WEEK ONE AND NEXT STEPS. Tuesday 9/1 is the first day for K, 6 and 9 only with orientation activities and afternoon teacher professional development; Wednesday 9/2 is an A Day half day for A-K in person with L-Z virtual; Thursday 9/3 is a B Day half day for L-Z in person with A-K virtual; Friday 9/4 is no school; Monday 9/7 is Labor Day; and Tuesday 9/8 is the first full day of school. The September calendar shown for 50% in-seat attendance marks the first day as 6th and 9th only, with all students virtual on Wednesdays September 16, 23 and 30. Next steps listed are a staff Q&A on Thursday, distribution of the presentation to parents Thursday with a question submission form, a Return to Learn Community Conversation on Monday, August 10 live on Facebook, a special Board meeting Wednesday, August 12 to approve the plan, and parents indicating interest in 100% virtual learning beginning Thursday the 13th with flexibility to make changes.
