**Identification**
Name of District: Troy School District. Address: 4400 Livernois, Troy, Michigan 48098. District Code Number: 63150. Web address: www.troy.k12.mi.us. Intermediate School District: Oakland Schools. Authorizing Body: Troy Board of Education. Plan dated August 12, 2020. Submitted by Richard M. Machesky, EdD., Superintendent of Schools.

**Legal framework**
Governor Whitmer's Executive Order 2020-142 requires districts to adopt a COVID-19 Preparedness and Response Plan across the phases of the Michigan Safe Start Plan, with the Michigan Return to School Roadmap supplying phase-appropriate safety protocols. Assurances include in-person instruction for students with disabilities consistent with their IEPs, good-faith equal access to alternative modes of instruction for students with disabilities from birth through age 26 including auxiliary services under section 1296 of the Revised School Code, MCL 380.1296, compliance with U.S. Department of Education and Michigan Department of Education guidance, individualized determinations on compensatory services for 2019-2020 closures, closure of buildings in Phases 1-3 except for defined personnel and licensed child-care providers, suspension of athletics and busing in Phases 1-3, continued employee pay, continued food distribution, and a Phase 4 prohibition on indoor assemblies bringing together students from more than one classroom.

**Instruction**
The task force totaled more than 105 members drawn from teachers, administrators, union representatives, and central office. Instructional elements include an updated pacing guide in Schoology, collaboration and professional learning time, MTSS team communication on each student's plan, monthly collaboration for general and special education teams on caseload students, and district MTSS expectations for new or in-process evaluation packets. Professional learning includes a Summer Homegrown Institute on anti-racist teaching, building community, and digital teaching, plus August grade-level learning on transitions between face-to-face and remote. All students K-12 will be provided an iPad; teachers receive an iPad kit; Schoology and ZOOM are the platforms. Scenarios mirror the Return to Learn plan: virtual in Phases 1-3, 50% in-seat in Phases 4/5, and 100% in-seat in Phases 4/5/6, with a return to regularly scheduled programming in September 2021.

**Health protocols**

| Area | Key requirement |
| --- | --- |
| Face coverings | Required at all times except eating; medical exemption needs a physician note, is logged in a master database, and is marked by an ID sticker |
| Hygiene | Posted classroom hygiene protocols, daily supply checks, first-day handwashing instruction reinforced weekly |
| Cleaning | EPA-approved disinfectant or diluted bleach; high-frequency areas wiped every four hours with time, date and initials charted; desks wiped after each exit or period |
| Screening | Isolation room no smaller than 100 square feet; trained quarantine officer; 5-minute interval activity log; 48-hour contact recall prioritizing sustained contact of 15 minutes or more |
| Exclusion | Staff positive test means 10 days from symptom onset plus 24 hours fever-free; close contacts excluded 14 days |
| Busing | Sanitizer mounts at each bus entrance, disposable masks at the door, ID sticker system, windows open when above 55 degrees F |

**Athletics**
Follows MHSAA guidelines and State of Michigan orders. Physicals on file for 2019-2020 carry over with an MHSAA questionnaire via FinalForms; Dr. Moeller recommends a physical and an electrocardiogram for any athlete proven to have had COVID-19. Practices use a 5-question survey, temperature check, masks, and 6 feet of distance. Low-risk sports (boys tennis, cross country with a maximum 70 runners, girls golf with a maximum 72 competitors at an 18-hole site, girls swim and dive) begin outdoor practices August 12; football began August 10 helmets-only with full pads August 17; MHSAA decisions on competition timelines were expected on or by August 20. Currently 100 spectators allowed, home-team only, no charge for entry, with games in stadiums and gyms live streamed through Pixellot/NFHS Network.

**Submission**
Due to the Board for approval by August 15 or seven days before the first day of school, adopted August 12, 2020, and transmitted by the ISD to the State Superintendent of Public Instruction and State Treasurer and posted to the district home page no later than August 17, 2020.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
COVID-19 Preparedness and Response Plan of the Troy School District, dated August 12, 2020, prepared to satisfy Governor Whitmer's Executive Order 2020-142 and titled internally TROY SCHOOL DISTRICT RETURN TO LEARN 2020-2021.

DISTRICT IDENTIFICATION. Name of District: Troy School District. Address of District: 4400 Livernois, Troy, Michigan 48098. District Code Number: 63150. Web address: www.troy.k12.mi.us. Name of Intermediate School District: Oakland Schools. Name of Authorizing Body: Troy Board of Education. Name of District leader submitting the plan: Richard M. Machesky, EdD., Superintendent of Schools.

INTRODUCTION. Executive Order 2020-142 provides a structure to support all schools in Michigan as they plan for a return of pre-K-12 education in the fall; under the order districts must adopt a COVID-19 Preparedness and Response Plan describing how they will cope with the disease across the phases of the Michigan Safe Start Plan, with the Michigan Return to School Roadmap offering a guide to safety protocols appropriate during each phase. The order notes there is no one-size-fits-all solution, that what works in Lansing may not work in Sault Sainte Marie, and that districts retain flexibility to tailor instruction to their needs and regional disease conditions.

ASSURANCES. The district agrees to meet the requirements of Executive Order 2020-142, assuring that when it provides in-person instruction to students without disabilities it will also provide in-person instruction to students with disabilities consistent with their individualized education programs; that when schools are closed to in-person instruction it will strive in good faith and to the extent practicable, based on available resources, technology, training and curriculum, to provide equal access to alternative modes of instruction to students with disabilities from birth through age 26, including auxiliary services under section 1296 of the Revised School Code, MCL 380.1296; that during any state of emergency or disaster related to the pandemic it will comply with guidance from the United States Department of Education including its Office of Civil Rights and Office of Special Education and Rehabilitative Services, and the Michigan Department of Education; that it will make individualized determinations on compensatory services for students with disabilities in light of the 2019-2020 school-year closures; that during Phases 1, 2 or 3 it will close buildings to anyone except district employees or contractors necessary for minimum basic school operations, food-service workers preparing food for distribution to students or families, and licensed child-care providers and the families they serve following state emergency protocols; that during Phases 1, 2 or 3 it will suspend athletics, after-school activities, inter-school activities and busing; that during those phases it will continue pay of school employees while redeploying staff, subject to collective bargaining agreements; that it will continue food distribution to eligible students; that during Phase 4 it will prohibit indoor assemblies bringing together students from more than one classroom; and that it will cooperate with the local public health department on confirmed cases, collecting contact information for close contacts from two days before symptoms to the time the individual was last present in school.

PHASE FRAMEWORK. The MI Safe Start Plan remains the highest-level governing framework. Schools may not provide in-person instruction of any kind in Phases 1-3; all schools may resume in-person instruction beginning in Phase 4; some regulations relax in Phase 5; and schools remain open with some lasting safety requirements in Phase 6. Schools retain authority to enact stricter public health requirements and to close buildings even if not mandated. Tribal Education Agencies and non-public schools are exempt from many state regulations but must adhere to Roadmap health and safety protocols. Phases 1-3 describe increasing and substantial community spread, concern about health system capacity, and testing and tracing that may be insufficient. Phase 4 describes falling new cases and deaths with case levels still high, most new outbreaks quickly identified, traced and contained, health system capacity able to handle outbreaks, and continued need for distancing. Phase 5 describes continued decreases, less common community infection, lower positivity rates with widespread testing, and rapid case investigation and containment.

INSTRUCTION. The district's goal is to have students return to face-to-face instruction as soon as possible while ensuring safety and sustainability with consistent programming, with Troy teachers leading learning and building nurturing classroom communities. The task force team included teachers, administrators, union representatives, and central office members totaling more than 105 members. Key instructional elements are an updated pacing guide and resources posted in Schoology; collaboration and professional learning time for teachers around curriculum and best practices; MTSS teams communicating on each student's plan to determine need and design plans; monthly collaboration time for general education and special education teacher teams regarding caseload students; and a district MTSS team creating expectations for receiving new packets or reviewing packets that were in process for evaluation for learning gaps. Professional learning includes the Summer Homegrown Institute on anti-racist teaching, building community and digital teaching, plus August grade-level professional learning on seamless transitions between face-to-face and remote experiences. Communication and family supports include Schoology as the consistent K-12 platform, opportunities for families to request translation services virtually, and parent training in Schoology and ZOOM.

TECHNOLOGY SUPPORT. All students K-12 will be provided with an iPad for at-home learning. Every teacher will have a dedicated iPad kit of tools including interactive stylus, keyboard and stand for live capture. K-12 instructional delivery is integrated into Schoology as the learning management system and ZOOM as the virtual platform. Technology gives students and families who choose or are scheduled to stay home direct access to the classroom through ZOOM; the virtual learning plan is connected to the in-seat plan with students logging in to their classroom through ZOOM, and there will be no separate, stand-alone virtual learning program.

SCENARIOS. Virtual Learning aligns to Phases 1-3, with 3 periods per day, live instruction via Zoom, and 100% virtual attendance. The Transition to Return Plan aligns to Phases 4/5 with 50% of students in-seat and 50% virtual, 3 periods per day, 90-minute classes for secondary, cohorting for in-seat attendance, buildings open 4 days for in-seat attendance, and all students attending virtually on Wednesdays. The In-Seat Learning Plan aligns to Phases 4/5/6 with 100% of students in-seat, 3 periods per day, 90-minute secondary classes, live instruction in person and via zoom, and buildings open for in-seat attendance all 5 days. Return to regularly scheduled programming is listed as September 2021. Elementary schedule components are literacy and math daily, science and social studies several times per week, access to all specials virtually, and built-in student support for at-risk learners and students with 504s and IEPs. Secondary components are an A Day (hours 1-3) / B Day (hours 4-6) schedule, 90-minute instructional blocks, student advisory, and student support for at-risk learners and students with 504s and IEPs. Notable virtual changes for Fall 2020 are a consistent schedule PreK through Post High, daily live Zoom instruction by all teachers, daily attendance, and regular student feedback PreK through Post High with academic grades in grades 6-12.

MENTAL AND SOCIAL EMOTIONAL HEALTH (PHASES 1-5). Schools will use the Student Risk Screening Survey (SRSS) three times per year to assess behavioral needs, with data reviewed by district and school MTSS teams and action plans created. Students will participate in a self-reporting universal mental health screener, and guidelines for identification and rapid referral of at-risk students are communicated to building-level support teams. Professional development for 2020-21 includes training in mental wellness, trauma informed teaching, student social emotional learning, and equity and inclusion, occurring over the course of the year. A School Mental Health professional is designated as the main contact to centralize mental health referrals and family communication, and also serves as liaison to local agencies and community partners. Compiled wellness resources include documents on student wellness and social emotional supports for families, the TSD Cares on-line referral for assistance, staff wellness resources, and the Employee Assistance Program (EAP). Crisis response is housed at the building level and includes grief and loss support; the School Mental Health building team will work with staff during staff meetings and establish a forum for staff wellness.

FACE COVERINGS. Staff, students and visitors must wear face coverings at all times except for eating, a requirement to be included in parent communications, handbooks, student orientations and staff orientations between August 1 and August 30. Students and parents must watch a safety video on wearing and maintaining face coverings and sign off before students may enter the classroom on the first day. Staff and students are expected to provide their own coverings; disposable coverings will be ordered and provided to anyone who forgets or cannot provide their own, with supply placed on buses and in each building by custodial and transportation staff by August 30. Individuals claiming medical exemption must provide their building office with a physician's note; exempted individuals will be recorded in a master database and issued a sticker for their student or staff ID. Staff will define, teach and prompt mask wearing within predictable school routines with daily re-teaching until routines are established. Students requiring special considerations such as 504 Plans, IEPs or health care plans will be referred to their case manager for additional interventions. Guests such as presenters and substitute teachers receive a disposable covering at sign-in, and non-compliance results in the guest being escorted from the building by the building administrator or law enforcement officer.

HYGIENE. Buildings will have adequate hand washing and hand sanitizer stations; supplies including paper towels, soap, hand sanitizer, tissues and trash receptacles are checked daily and restocked in classrooms, with teachers contacting the office immediately if supplies run low. Each classroom will post a hygiene protocol with a hand-washing schedule and a room and materials cleaning schedule. Teachers or the school nurse teach proper handwashing and cough and sneeze etiquette on the first day of school, reinforced weekly or more often, possibly by video. The Operations Department procures soap, hand sanitizer, paper towels and tissues routinely, posts signage, monitors supplies, and procures hand sanitizing stations in collaboration with building leadership.

CLEANING. District-level administrators and building operations will review guidance and the Building Operations sections of the MI Safe Schools: Michigan's 2020-21 Return to School Roadmap. An inventory of cleaning supplies compliant with EPA-approved COVID-19 materials will be taken and orders placed. All buildings receive EPA-approved disinfectant or diluted bleach solution, paper towels, face shields and gloves; staff or students must wear gloves, a mask and face shield when cleaning. Each building custodial team and administrator will tour the building, identify frequent-use areas, and create a map kept secure in the head custodian room and office for use by custodial substitutes. Custodial staff will wipe all high-frequency usage areas every four hours and following any evening activities, noting time, date and initials on a daily chart. Student desks will be wiped every time students exit the room at elementary level, or after every period at secondary level, with EPA-approved disinfectant or diluted bleach solution accessible from each classroom.

ATHLETICS. The plan follows all MHSAA-recommended guidelines and State of Michigan orders. Student-athletes with a sports physical on file for 2019-2020 do not need a new physical for 2020-2021 but must complete the MHSAA sports questionnaire on FinalForms and submit it to their coach or athletic trainer before practice or tryouts; those without a physical on file must complete and print the form from FinalForms. As recommended by Dr. Moeller, any student-athlete proven to have had COVID-19 should have a sports physical and an electrocardiogram (ECG) to rule out myocarditis, with full recommendations on both high school athletic websites and sent to parents on voluntary summer practice rosters. Practice check-in follows summer workout procedures: a 5-question survey, temperature check, masks worn by all student-athletes and coaches during check-in, and 6 feet of distance before and after practice. Masks must be worn before and after practice and equipment cleaned during and after. Only the football team has limited locker room use due to equipment needs, with players reporting dressed; all other teams report ready, and bathrooms are used one at a time. The weight room remains closed until allowed to open by the Governor, weights may be used outdoors and must be cleaned between use. Athletes bring their own water bottles with no sharing, no hydration stations and no snacks; no spectators at practice. For games, all athletes, coaches and game workers follow the same check-in, coaches, workers and bench personnel wear masks, visiting teams do not use locker rooms, only the home football team has limited locker room use, and players bring their own water or small disposable bottles are provided with a trained adult in PPE operating any water station. Concession stands are a local health department decision. If parents are not allowed to attend games, two-way busing will be provided; student-athletes may drive themselves with parent permission and a signed release, and parents may drive their child to an away game. Clarification was pending from the Governor on how cheerleaders and marching band members count toward maximum capacity. Under OAA rules, spectators are a home team decision, only home team spectators would be allowed, currently 100 spectators are allowed, the plan is for no charge for entry, and all games played in stadiums and gyms will be live streamed through Pixellot/NFHS Network.

COVID POSITIVE PROTOCOL. A more complete version appears on page five of the MHSAA sports return to play documents. Steps: contact the building administrator, central office administrator and health department and follow guidance; close contacts may have to quarantine for 14 days, with close contact defined as anyone less than six feet apart for more than 15 minutes at any point from two days before symptoms until the individual is isolated; notify all schools, families and officials involved without identifying the person; monitor those present but not in close contact for symptoms, who may not need testing; and clean the area.

FALL SPORTS GUIDANCE. Low-risk sports: boys tennis begins outdoor practices August 12 with no more than four teams at one site (JV and varsity count as two teams) and larger invitationals likely canceled; cross country begins August 12 with a maximum of 70 runners allowed in a race and spectator capacity difficult to monitor; girls golf begins August 12 with a maximum of 72 competitors at an 18-hole site; girls swim and dive begins outdoor practices August 12 pending the Governor on indoor training, with no more than four teams at one site. Moderate- and high-risk sports: boys soccer begins August 12 with no more than four teams at one site and an MHSAA decision on competition timelines anticipated on or by August 20; boys water polo is not an MHSAA sport and was moved to spring by the MWPA; football begins practices August 10 with helmets only for an acclimation week, permits 7 on 7, handoffs, blocking pads and sleds, allows full pads beginning August 17, with an MHSAA timeline decision anticipated on or by August 20; sideline cheer begins outdoor practice August 12 with its counting toward stadium capacity undetermined; volleyball begins outdoor practices August 12 pending the Governor on indoor training, with no more than four teams at one site. Regional and state meets were being investigated by MHSAA for several sports.

SCREENING AND TESTING. The district will comply with the health, screening and testing guidance and requirements of the Oakland County COVID-19 Public Health Toolkit for K-12 Schools. All school staff and students must conduct a health safety self-assessment at home before coming to work. Each building will identify a remote and secluded room no smaller than 100 square feet as an isolation area outfitted with appropriate PPE, and will have an identified and trained quarantine officer whose duties take precedence over other responsibilities. From identification of potential infection the student will not be left unattended, with a log sheet of activity maintained at 5-minute intervals until the student or staff member is safely removed. Parent communication is immediate with directions on pick-up and testing; designated office staff contact the family daily until test results are provided and verified before return. During quarantine the student self-identifies locations and individuals contacted over the past 48 hours, prioritizing sustained contact of 15 minutes or more; the health department is contacted after parents to assist with contact tracing. Staff unable to work due to symptoms must report it, with the school health official or Employee Services Department monitoring daily and directing testing. A positive test for a staff member requires quarantine away from school for 10 days since symptoms first appeared, 24 hours with no fever, and improvement of symptoms. Household members, classmates and teachers of the quarantined person who are close contacts are excluded for 14 days after their last date of close contact.

BUSING AND STUDENT TRANSPORTATION. All transportation companies supporting the district will be contacted to confirm receipt of the MI Safe Schools Roadmap criteria; a meeting will review Phase 4 criteria; contracting companies will sign an assurance statement; and contracts will be altered as needed to address cleaning, sanitizing and professional development. The transportation department will assess the number of buses on the road. Buses will be fitted with mounts for hand sanitizer at the entrance. Contractors will use CDC-compliant cleaning supplies between routes including frequent-contact areas, and disposable face masks will be placed at the bus entrance each morning. A mandatory face covering policy for buses will be communicated to families, if medically feasible, unless it is determined case by case that it is not safe for the bus driver to wear a facial covering. Bus drivers will be informed of the ID badge sticker system for students medically unable to wear a mask, and all students will show their ID as they board. Driver training covers appropriate use of face covering, policies on face covering and hand sanitizing, and cleaning and disinfecting methods. Weather permitting, defined as no precipitation and temperature above 55 degrees F, drivers will keep windows open en route and when stopped. On buses with specialized transportation and equipment needs, aides or drivers will wipe down equipment before use.

SUBMISSION. Each district must submit a single completed Assurance Document and Preparedness Plan to its Board of Education in time for approval by August 15 or seven days before the first day of school, whichever comes first. This plan was adopted by the Troy School District Board of Education at a Special Board Meeting held on August 12, 2020, with signature lines for the Board of Education President and date. The Preparedness Plan will be collected by the Intermediate School District for transmission to the State Superintendent of Public Instruction and State Treasurer by August 17, 2020, and must be posted on the district's public website home page no later than August 17, 2020, with a single application filed by the district rather than multiple applications for individual schools.

RESOLUTION 20-064, PLEDGE FOR RACIAL EQUITY. Moved by Dr. Philippart and supported by Mr. Hauff. The pledge recites three commitments. First, that the Troy School District will continue to make communities and workplaces trusting places by having complex, and sometimes difficult, conversations about racism, diversity, equity and inclusion, creating and maintaining environments, platforms and forums where residents feel comfortable reaching out to colleagues to gain greater awareness of each other's experiences and perspectives, encouraging ongoing dialogue and not tolerating incongruence with these values of openness, thereby building trust, encouraging compassion and open-mindedness, and reinforcing a commitment to a culture of inclusivity that acknowledges racism as real and pursues equity through racially conscious approaches. Second, that the district will implement and expand implicit bias education, noting that the field of implicit bias reminds us that we all have unconscious biases and that such education enables individuals and institutions to recognize, acknowledge and engage in debiasing strategies, with a commitment to rolling out or expanding implicit bias education within local municipalities and institutions to help employees, students and residents recognize blind spots. Third, that the district will share best and unsuccessful practices, since many local jurisdictions are at different stages in increasing racial consciousness and cultural awareness, committing to identify best successes and least successful initiatives to share with others, to create accountability systems within communities and institutions to measure, monitor and evaluate progress, and to share regular updates with the Equity Office of the Michigan Department of Civil Rights in order to catalog effective programs and measurement practices. The pledge concludes that these three goals are not the complete answer but are concrete steps toward more equitable workplaces and communities, that working together toward equity can cultivate racially conscious change that anticipates unintended outcomes and does not rely on good intentions but on awareness that all have work to do to dismantle systems of advantage embedded in cultural mindsets and practices that sustain racial inequity, and affirms the value of human diversity and inclusion in all its forms, recognizing that communities have been impacted by racialized messages that contribute to the formation of unconscious biases, and stating opposition to discrimination. **Memorandum of June 14, 2019**
To Rick West, Assistant Superintendent, Business Services, from Beth Soggs, Director of Technology, Technology Services, 4420 Livernois, Troy, MI 48098, phone 248.823.5060, regarding High School 1:1 Implementation. A pilot one to one program was conducted during the first semester of the 2018-19 school year with 10th and 11th grade students and 12 teachers at Athens and Troy High Schools. Informational surveys gathered input from pilot teachers, non-pilot teachers, students, and parents; student work was reviewed for evidence supporting the blue pillar district goals. The memorandum recommends phasing in with 9th grade students and 9th grade teachers at the start of the 2019-20 school year, because that allows a full school year to evaluate a fully implemented 1:1 environment, focused professional learning with a smaller group of teachers, and continuity for students who used an iPad in 8th grade, now with a keyboard. Recommended plan: 2019-20, iPads for all 9th graders; Spring 2020, program evaluation - if positive, phase-in continues with each incoming 9th grade class; if negative, the iPads purchased will be used to refresh 3rd grade iPads the following year as planned. The purchase from Apple Computers with REMC bid pricing for 1050 iPads with keyboard cases is $367,500; it must be made prior to June 21, 2019 to receive this special pricing, and after June 21, 2019 the cost for 1050 devices will increase to $412,650.

**Report: TSD 1:1 High School Digital Learning Environment, May 7, 2019**
Submitted by Jennifer Gottlieb and Beth Soggs. The rationale quotes Fullan & Quinn ("Leveraging digital is not about devices but about learning that can be amplified, accelerated, and facilitated by interaction with the digital world") and Fullan, Quinn, & McEachen on deep learning partnerships with students, families, community members, and experts regardless of geographical location. Troy School District has an established 1:1 iPad program for grades 3-8; a high school 1:1 environment would let students deepen learning, connect and collaborate locally and globally, receive timely feedback, and lighten backpacks since most textbooks also provide electronic access. Bond money has been set aside to support this initiative. The Teaching and Learning Cabinet found stakeholders split between iPad and laptop, but pilot teachers reported iPads offer more opportunities to amplify deep learning, aligning with the Core Value of Deepening Learning; the Cabinet therefore recommends iPads for all high school students. Cost for 2019-20 is approximately $350,000 ($350 for iPad/case x 1000 9th grade students); the slide deck adds a total cost over 4 years of $1,400,000. iPads will be purchased during the summer of 2019, with professional learning planned with the pilot teachers, the high school tech chairs, and the Teaching and Learning Department.

**Table 1: Process for Moving Toward a HS 1:1 Digital Learning Environment**
Spanning 2017-18 to 2019-20: Fall, the Technology Leadership Team (TLT) decides to explore a high school 1:1 environment; January, Student Survey; February, TLT shares results and vision with Board; March, Teacher Survey; April, pilot applications open; June, pilot teachers selected; August, 1:1 pilot begins in 12 classrooms at Athens and Troy High; January, pilot ends with student work collected and teachers and students surveyed; February, pilot teachers present at staff meetings, focus group interviews at both high schools, Teacher Survey; March, progress shared with Board, cost of alternate devices explored, student focus groups, TLT review meeting, Parent Survey; April, pilot teacher follow-up comparing a new laptop to iPads, non-pilot teachers test both, Teaching and Learning Cabinet makes its final recommendation; May, seek Board approval; Summer, devices purchased; August, professional learning for all 9th grade teachers; Spring, program evaluation.

**Table 2: Results**
January 2018 Student Survey (N=1248): students have access to devices at home but only 62% have a desktop, laptop, or tablet for their exclusive use; most bring phones to school; classroom technology use drops from middle school to high school. March 2018 Teacher Survey (N = 98): 1:1 promotes equity and would increase opportunities to engage, collaborate, receive feedback, access resources, and create; the cart system is not sufficient; teachers worry about distractions. January 2019 Pilot Project Student Work: shows promise in attaining the "blue pillar" and suggests students are learning more. January 2019 Pilot Project Teacher Survey (N = 12 pilot teachers): Modified BYOD was extremely difficult to navigate and support; teachers overwhelmingly prefer the iPad, citing apps that support deeper learning outcomes, Apple Classroom, locked browsers, and ease of use. January 2019 Pilot Project Student Survey (N = 244 pilot students): students prefer the Windows Laptop or Modified BYOD environment for familiarity and freedom. February 2019 Teacher Focus Groups at Athens and Troy High: unanimously against BYOD, favored iPads, noted the benefit of the same device each day. February 2019 Teacher Survey (N = 156): laptop/iPad carts and the current BYOD program are not sustainable; a hands-on year-long professional learning plan is needed. March 2019 Parent Survey (N = 426): on a scale of 0 (no support) to 100 (highest support), the average score was 74; concerns include teacher preparation, monitoring device use at home, and excessive exposure to technology. March 2019 exploration of alternate Windows devices at the Board's request found they would incur an ongoing general fund expenditure of $16,000 annually for device management similar to Apple Classroom. March 2019 student meetings found WiFi problems were due to filtering and student VPN use rather than the network; students did not support iPads, largely perceiving them as a middle school device. A Technology Leadership Team meeting on March 25, 2019 reviewed the survey data. April 2019 pilot teacher follow-up found the Windows laptop camera limited to 30 frames per second, causing blurry video, while iPad cameras run 60-120 frames per second; video upload was slow on Windows; the Windows keyboard is easier for typing; instant-on iPads were more versatile for quick assessments. Non-pilot teacher testing found laptops preferred by students especially for typing, long battery life on both, and concern about Windows device durability.
